questions.question: A woman has intermittent diplopia and ptosis that worsen during prolonged reading. Sustained upgaze increases the ptosis; pupils, sensation and tendon reflexes are normal. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Thyroid-associated orbitopathy
Autoimmune myasthenia gravis
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia
An isolated third-nerve palsy
questions.explanation:
Objective Fatigability in Myasthenia Gravis

Correct answer: Autoimmune myasthenia gravis

Transmission Failure Rather Than General Fatigue

**MG causes fluctuating objective skeletal-muscle weakness**, particularly ocular, bulbar, neck and proximal limb weakness. Repeated activity can reveal a decrement in performance, with improvement after rest.

General tiredness alone is insufficient. Demonstrate a reproducible pattern and ask about chewing, speech, swallowing, head control and breathing as well as limb activity.

Pupillary responses and sensation are generally preserved. Prominent autonomic symptoms or areflexia should broaden the differential to presynaptic disease and other mimics.

Confirm and Determine Extent

**Serology and appropriately selected electrophysiology** support a compatible phenotype. Ocular-only disease can have negative standard antibody and routine stimulation results, so one negative test is not an automatic exclusion.

Assess for generalization and airway risk at the first encounter. Severe dysphagia, weak cough or respiratory decline needs urgent evaluation rather than a routine outpatient diagnostic sequence.

Evaluate thymic disease after autoimmune MG is established. Symptomatic acetylcholinesterase inhibition and immune treatment have different roles; response to a drug trial alone should not replace diagnostic concordance. Fixed ophthalmoplegia, restrictive eye movements or a focal cranial-nerve pattern warrant targeted assessment for competing pathology.

Thyroid-associated orbitopathy: Orbitopathy can cause diplopia through restrictive extraocular disease, often with lid retraction or proptosis; fluctuating fatigable ptosis with this examination is more characteristic of MG.

Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia: Mitochondrial ophthalmoplegia can produce ptosis and ocular weakness, but usually progresses slowly with relatively fixed limitation rather than clear activity-related fluctuation.

An isolated third-nerve palsy: A third-nerve lesion can cause ptosis and diplopia, sometimes with pupil involvement; a consistent nerve-pattern deficit rather than fluctuating fatigability would be expected.

AAPM&R: myasthenia gravis, updated 2024 — https://now.aapmr.org/myasthenia-gravis/

International consensus guidance for MG: 2020 update, published 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000011124

questions.question: An adult has convincing fatigable bulbar and neck weakness. Standard AChR antibodies are negative. Which antibody assay is most appropriate next in the usual autoimmune MG evaluation?
options: Anti-HMGCR antibodies
P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies
Anti-GQ1b IgG
MuSK antibodies
questions.explanation:
Antibody Testing After a Negative AChR Assay

Correct answer: MuSK antibodies

A Phenotype-Directed Sequence

**AChR antibodies are the commonest autoimmune MG marker.** If the standard assay is negative and clinical suspicion persists, test MuSK, especially in prominent bulbar, neck or respiratory disease.

A negative result does not establish absence of autoimmunity. Specialist testing can include clustered-AChR cell-based assays and selected LRP4 evaluation, interpreted according to assay validation and the clinical setting.

Avoid treating every weak antibody signal as diagnostic. False positives and unrelated antibodies become more consequential when the clinical pretest probability is low.

Seronegative Is a Test Description

**Seronegative MG requires the same clinical discipline** as seropositive disease. Targeted RNS or jitter testing can support impaired neuromuscular transmission, while reassessment should exclude myopathy, motor neuron disease and structural causes.

Early-onset, familial or atypical persistent disease can suggest a congenital myasthenic syndrome even when recognized in adulthood. Genetic syndromes need subtype-directed treatment rather than automatic immune escalation.

Antibody subgroup helps guide later therapy, but the clinical severity determines urgency. Do not delay airway assessment or rescue treatment for a convincing severe exacerbation while awaiting a specialized assay. Antibody concentration alone is not a reliable substitute for serial strength, bulbar and respiratory assessment.

Anti-HMGCR antibodies: HMGCR antibodies identify an immune necrotizing myopathy context, usually with persistent proximal weakness and substantial CK elevation, not primarily fatigable bulbar transmission failure.

P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies: These support LEMS in a compatible proximal, autonomic and reflex-facilitation phenotype; they are not the usual next autoimmune MG assay for prominent fatigable bulbar-neck weakness.

Anti-GQ1b IgG: GQ1b testing is relevant to acute ophthalmoplegic/ataxic GBS-spectrum disease, especially with areflexia; it does not investigate the most likely MG subgroup here.

questions.question: Which mechanism most closely characterizes the commonly IgG4-mediated MuSK-associated form of MG?
options: Genetically reduced acetylcholinesterase anchoring at the end plate
Complement-mediated destruction by antibodies binding the AChR as the principal process
Antibody-mediated reduction of presynaptic calcium entry
Disruption of agrin–LRP4–MuSK signaling and AChR clustering
questions.explanation:
MuSK Antibodies and Receptor Clustering

Correct answer: Disruption of agrin–LRP4–MuSK signaling and AChR clustering

Postsynaptic Organization

**MuSK coordinates postsynaptic specialization** through the agrin–LRP4 signaling pathway. Interference reduces effective clustering and stability of AChRs, compromising the safety margin of transmission.

The predominance of IgG4 helps explain why complement-mediated injury is not the same central mechanism as in common AChR-antibody disease. Antibody specificity therefore has therapeutic as well as diagnostic importance.

Clinical presentations often emphasize facial, bulbar, neck and respiratory muscles, sometimes with less prominent limb weakness. This is a tendency rather than a requirement for every patient.

Clinical Consequences

**Pyridostigmine may be less effective or less well tolerated** in MuSK MG, so a poor symptomatic response should prompt clinical reassessment rather than dismissal of a supported diagnosis.

Rituximab is an early consideration after an unsatisfactory response to initial immunotherapy under international consensus guidance. The evidence and indications for targeted therapies must be checked for the relevant antibody subgroup.

Thymectomy evidence from nonthymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG should not be transferred automatically to MuSK disease. A thymic mass still needs its own assessment. In severe bulbar disease, secretion handling and ventilatory reserve require attention even when limb strength appears relatively preserved.

Target | Relevant mechanism | Clinical implication

AChR | Postsynaptic receptor loss/blockade and complement-mediated injury | AChR-specific evidence for thymectomy and selected C5 inhibitors

MuSK | Disrupted clustering signaling; often IgG4 | Bulbar/neck phenotype and early rituximab consideration

P/Q-type VGCC | Reduced presynaptic calcium-dependent release | LEMS phenotype, facilitation and cancer evaluation

Genetically reduced acetylcholinesterase anchoring at the end plate: COLQ-related congenital disease can impair acetylcholinesterase anchoring and alter transmission, but is an inherited syndrome rather than MuSK autoantibody disease.

Complement-mediated destruction by antibodies binding the AChR as the principal process: Complement-fixing AChR antibodies can damage the postsynaptic membrane in AChR MG; MuSK IgG4 disease primarily interferes with receptor-clustering signaling.

Antibody-mediated reduction of presynaptic calcium entry: Presynaptic P/Q-type calcium-channel autoimmunity is characteristic of LEMS and reduces acetylcholine release; it is not the MuSK receptor-clustering mechanism.

International consensus guidance for MG: 2020 update, published 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000011124

Guideline for management of myasthenic syndromes, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1177/17562864231213240

questions.question: In the conventional low-frequency RNS protocol for suspected MG, approximately what reproducible first-to-fourth/fifth CMAP decrement is commonly considered abnormal after technical artifacts are excluded?
options: At least 30%
At least 3%
At least 20%
At least 10%
questions.explanation:
Low-Frequency Repetitive Nerve Stimulation

Correct answer: At least 10%

Measure Failure Across Repeated Stimuli

**Low-frequency RNS**, commonly at 2–3 Hz, tests the stability of neuromuscular transmission. A conventional abnormal result is a reproducible decrement of at least about ==10%== under the specified laboratory protocol.

Maintain adequate temperature, immobilization and supramaximal stimulation. Movement, changing activation and unstable baseline recording can produce misleading amplitude changes.

Test clinically involved muscles. Facial or proximal recordings can improve yield when distal hand recordings are normal, particularly in an ocular-bulbar presentation.

Interpret Sensitivity and Specificity

**A positive decrement supports transmission failure rather than a unique etiology.** Combine the result with clinical findings, antibody tests and relevant postexercise testing.

Sensitivity is lower in restricted ocular disease, and an unrevealing limited study does not exclude MG. Targeted jitter testing may be appropriate when suspicion remains high.

A normal routine sensory study is expected in an isolated NMJ disorder, but coexisting neuropathy can complicate the overall electrodiagnostic picture. Document medications and laboratory instructions; do not independently stop essential therapy in a patient at respiratory risk simply to improve test yield.

At least 30%: Thirty percent is used in selected motor conduction-block frameworks with other qualifications, not as the conventional low-frequency NMJ decrement threshold.

At least 3%: Small response variation can occur from measurement and technical factors; three percent is below the conventional decrement threshold specified in this question.

At least 20%: A decrement this large is abnormal, but requiring it would miss responses between the conventional threshold and twenty percent; the question asks the threshold, not a more severe example.

AANEM practice parameter: RNS and single-fiber EMG in suspected MG/LEMS — https://www.aanem.org/docs/default-source/documents/aanem/practice/guidelines/myastheniagravis_reaffirmed.pdf

AAPM&R: myasthenia gravis, updated 2024 — https://now.aapmr.org/myasthenia-gravis/

questions.question: A patient has repeatedly documented fatigable ptosis and diplopia, negative standard AChR/MuSK assays and normal routine distal-hand RNS. Which test is most useful next to assess neuromuscular transmission?
options: Postexercise increment testing in distal hand muscles
Conventional needle EMG of clinically involved facial and proximal muscles
Blink-reflex studies with facial motor conduction
Jitter testing in an appropriately selected clinically involved facial muscle
questions.explanation:
Jitter Testing After Nondiagnostic RNS

Correct answer: Jitter testing in an appropriately selected clinically involved facial muscle

Measure Variability in Transmission

**Single-fiber EMG or validated concentric-needle jitter testing** measures variation in the timing of muscle-fiber responses. Increased jitter and blocking support impaired neuromuscular transmission.

Use muscle- and technique-specific reference values. Stimulated and voluntary recordings have different protocols, so a single universal microsecond cutoff should not be applied to every method.

Test selection matters: a normal distal-hand study can be less informative when the clinical disorder is predominantly ocular. Temperature, activation stability, sampling and recent treatment influence interpretation.

Sensitive Does Not Mean Etiologically Specific

**Abnormal jitter does not independently diagnose autoimmune MG.** Reinnervation, some myopathies, presynaptic disease and botulinum toxin exposure can produce abnormalities.

Interpret the conventional EMG and clinical pattern alongside jitter, antibody assays and history. An isolated borderline result in a patient with nonspecific fatigue has a different meaning from a marked abnormality in reproducible ocular fatigability.

A technically adequate normal study in an appropriately weak muscle lowers the probability of transmission failure, but does not justify an absolute exclusion from an inadequately sampled or treated case. Confirm the diagnosis before committing a seronegative patient to prolonged immune treatment, and reassess structural, mitochondrial or congenital alternatives when the pattern remains discordant.

Postexercise increment testing in distal hand muscles: Postexercise testing is useful when presynaptic LEMS is suspected; a targeted facial jitter study more directly addresses this persistent ocular postsynaptic suspicion.

Conventional needle EMG of clinically involved facial and proximal muscles: Conventional EMG helps identify myopathic or neurogenic mimics, but targeted jitter is more sensitive for transmission instability when routine stimulation has been unrevealing.

Blink-reflex studies with facial motor conduction: These can investigate selected brainstem, trigeminal or facial pathway disorders; they do not provide the same assessment of endplate timing variability in suspected ocular MG.

questions.question: An adult has fluctuating unilateral ptosis with normal pupils. After an ice pack is applied to the closed eyelid for two minutes, the lid position improves objectively by 3 mm. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: It increases the likelihood of aponeurotic ptosis
It increases the likelihood of ocular MG in this clinical context
It increases the likelihood of mitochondrial external ophthalmoplegia
It increases the likelihood of restrictive thyroid orbitopathy
questions.explanation:
Ice-Pack Testing for Ptosis

Correct answer: It increases the likelihood of ocular MG in this clinical context

A Practical Supportive Bedside Test

**Cooling can transiently improve myasthenic ptosis.** Measure lid position before and after a standardized short application, protecting skin and avoiding pressure on the globe.

A commonly used positive criterion is improvement of about ==2 mm or more==, but protocols and baseline severity affect performance. Document an objective change rather than a vague impression.

The test is most useful when ptosis is present. Its interpretation is less straightforward for isolated diplopia, and a negative result does not exclude all ocular MG.

Keep the Differential and Disease Extent in View

**Fatigability, pupil examination and ocular-movement pattern** help distinguish MG from cranial neuropathy, restrictive orbitopathy and fixed muscle or eyelid disease.

Pain, anisocoria, an acute focal nerve pattern or other concerning signs require appropriate urgent investigation. A bedside test must not distract from an aneurysmal or other structural emergency.

Use antibody testing and selected electrophysiology according to the overall probability. Ask about swallowing, chewing, speech, neck and limb function and breathing. Ocular symptoms can precede generalization; neither a positive ice test nor a normal limb examination predicts permanent ocular restriction.

It increases the likelihood of aponeurotic ptosis: Aponeurotic disease causes structural lid elevation failure, whereas an objective transient improvement after cooling in fluctuating ptosis is more supportive of impaired transmission.

It increases the likelihood of mitochondrial external ophthalmoplegia: Mitochondrial ophthalmoplegia can produce ptosis but usually has a slowly progressive fixed course; this dynamic bedside response more strongly supports the myasthenic differential.

It increases the likelihood of restrictive thyroid orbitopathy: Thyroid orbitopathy can cause diplopia and lid abnormalities, but mechanical restriction is not the expected explanation for the stated reversible fatigable ptosis response.

questions.question: A 45-year-old with newly confirmed AChR-positive generalized MG has no chest symptoms and a normal chest radiograph. Which investigation should assess associated thymic disease?
options: Chest radiography with interval reassessment
Cross-sectional thoracic imaging with CT, or MRI when appropriate
Whole-body FDG-PET as the initial screening study
Striational-antibody profiling before deciding whether to image
questions.explanation:
Thymic Imaging in Autoimmune MG

Correct answer: Cross-sectional thoracic imaging with CT, or MRI when appropriate

Look for a Clinically Silent Thymoma

**Thymoma may be asymptomatic**, so a normal chest history and radiograph are insufficient to exclude it. Thoracic CT is commonly used; MRI is an alternative or problem-solving study when appropriate.

Imaging assesses a mediastinal mass and helps distinguish other thymic appearances. Thymic hyperplasia and thymoma have different implications and should not be treated as synonymous.

Thyroid and other autoimmune associations can also be relevant, but their evaluation does not replace investigation of the thymus.

Separate Oncologic and Immunologic Indications

**A thymoma requires multidisciplinary tumor assessment**, with surgery when indicated by resectability and the patient’s clinical condition. Stabilize significant MG before an elective operation.

The immunologic benefit of thymectomy in selected nonthymomatous AChR-positive generalized disease is a separate evidence-based indication. Its age, phenotype and timing considerations should not be confused with treating a tumor.

Thymectomy is not an immediate rescue for crisis, and improvement in autoimmune disease can be delayed. Continue appropriate perioperative medication, respiratory planning and follow-up. Antibody subgroup, comorbidity and operative risk inform decisions when no tumor is present; do not assume that every seronegative or MuSK-positive patient gains the same benefit.

Chest radiography with interval reassessment: Radiography can reveal a large mass but is insufficient to exclude clinically silent thymoma; cross-sectional imaging is the appropriate anatomical evaluation.

Whole-body FDG-PET as the initial screening study: PET has selected tumor-assessment roles but is not the usual first-line substitute for anatomical thymic CT or MRI in this setting.

Striational-antibody profiling before deciding whether to image: Striational antibodies can accompany thymoma-associated or late-onset MG, but cannot reliably replace anatomical assessment or safely gate imaging on their result.

questions.question: A patient with MG has severe dysphagia requiring a feeding tube and predominantly bulbar weakness, but has not required intubation. Which MGFA clinical class best fits?
options: Class V
Class IIIb
Class IVa
Class IVb
questions.explanation:
MGFA Clinical Class and Bulbar Severity

Correct answer: Class IVb

Classify Distribution and Severity

**MGFA clinical classes** describe current clinical severity and distribution. Ocular weakness can accompany generalized classes, and the worst affected nonocular domain determines the generalized category.

The a subclasses emphasize limb/axial involvement, whereas b subclasses emphasize oropharyngeal/respiratory involvement. Assess function directly rather than inferring severity from antibody concentration.

Feeding-tube dependence without intubation is specifically included in IVb. Routine postoperative intubation does not, by itself, change the clinical class to V.

Do Not Confuse a Class With a Treatment Goal

**Clinical class is different from postintervention status**, minimal manifestations or remission. The MG-ADL and other scales serve complementary longitudinal purposes and are not interchangeable labels.

A patient can deteriorate urgently within a class. Weak cough, secretion difficulty or falling ventilatory reserve needs action before an intubation-based category is reached.

Document bulbar, respiratory, axial and limb findings with serial functional measures. Clinical response and medication adverse effects guide treatment adjustment; a class number alone does not specify one mandatory drug or determine whether the patient can safely remain outside monitored care.

Class | Clinical framework

I | Ocular weakness only; eye closure weakness may occur

II | Mild generalized weakness; a limb/axial, b bulbar/respiratory predominance

III | Moderate generalized weakness; a/b distribution subclasses

IV | Severe generalized weakness; a/b subclasses; feeding tube without intubation is IVb

V | Intubation, except routine postoperative management

Class V: Class V is defined by intubation outside routine postoperative management in the standard MGFA clinical classification; a feeding tube without intubation is specifically IVb.

Class IIIb: Class IIIb denotes moderate generalized disease with predominantly oropharyngeal/respiratory involvement; severe bulbar disease requiring tube feeding without intubation belongs to IVb.

Class IVa: Class IVa denotes severe generalized disease with predominantly limb or axial involvement; the severe bulbar predominance here places the patient in the b subclass.

questions.question: An adult with newly diagnosed mild generalized MG has no significant bulbar or respiratory involvement. Which medicine is used for rapid symptomatic improvement by reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition?
options: Pyridostigmine
Amifampridine
Prednisolone
Azathioprine
questions.explanation:
Pyridostigmine Is Symptomatic Therapy

Correct answer: Pyridostigmine

Increase Acetylcholine Availability

**Pyridostigmine prolongs acetylcholine action** at the NMJ and can improve strength within a dose interval. It treats symptoms rather than eliminating the autoimmune process.

A common adult starting approach is ==30 mg three or four times daily==, titrated to benefit and tolerability. Individualize timing to activities and meals; a rigid escalating dose is not a substitute for reassessing disease control.

Patients with significant bulbar or respiratory weakness require urgent severity-directed care. Increasing oral symptomatic medication alone does not treat an impending crisis.

Recognize Cholinergic Adverse Effects

**Diarrhea, abdominal cramps, salivation, sweating and bradycardia** reflect muscarinic effects; excessive exposure can also cause fasciculation and weakness.

Mechanical intestinal or urinary obstruction is a contraindication. Use caution with asthma and clinically important bradyarrhythmia; renal impairment can require lower individualized doses.

Review dose-related symptoms and objective strength before assuming every decline is autoimmune worsening. Persistent functional weakness despite tolerated dosing warrants immune-treatment assessment. MuSK-associated disease can respond less well or tolerate treatment poorly. Antimuscarinic symptom treatment does not remove nicotinic toxicity or justify continued excessive dosing; the overall clinical and respiratory state remains the priority.

Amifampridine: Amifampridine increases presynaptic acetylcholine release through potassium-channel blockade and is a principal symptomatic treatment for LEMS, not the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor requested here.

Prednisolone: Prednisolone provides immune treatment for MG with a slower clinical course and possible initial worsening; its action is not reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition.

Azathioprine: Azathioprine is a delayed-onset steroid-sparing immunosuppressant used in selected MG patients; it does not provide the rapid synaptic symptomatic effect described.

questions.question: A patient with confirmed ocular MG has persistent disabling diplopia despite an adequate tolerated pyridostigmine trial. There is no respiratory or bulbar involvement. Which immune-treatment approach is generally recommended initially?
options: Begin azathioprine monotherapy
Begin regularly scheduled IVIG maintenance
Introduce corticosteroid therapy with an individualized low-dose escalation and monitoring plan
Refer for nonthymomatous thymectomy as the initial immune intervention
questions.explanation:
Functionally Limiting Ocular MG

Correct answer: Introduce corticosteroid therapy with an individualized low-dose escalation and monitoring plan

Treat Functional Limitation

**Troublesome ptosis or ophthalmoparesis despite acetylcholinesterase inhibition** can justify immunotherapy. International consensus recommends corticosteroids as the initial immune agent in this setting.

Assess the effect on reading, mobility, work and driving rather than treating an antibody titer. Reconsider the diagnosis when eye movements are fixed or restrictive, or the clinical response is discordant.

A low starting dose with gradual escalation may improve tolerability and reduce early worsening risk in a stable outpatient. The optimal schedule is individualized rather than a single universally proven regimen.

Balance Benefit and Toxicity

**Use the lowest effective exposure** and monitor glucose, BP, weight, mood, infection and bone risk. Significant bulbar or respiratory disease changes the setting and may require rapid rescue therapy.

If steroids are contraindicated, poorly tolerated or insufficient, consider an appropriate steroid-sparing agent with counseling about delayed onset and laboratory monitoring.

Support diplopia temporarily with selected occlusion or optical measures where appropriate, and reassess for generalization. Established symptomatic benefit and immune control are different outcomes. Evidence for ocular therapy includes small trials and consensus; do not claim that corticosteroids guarantee prevention of future generalization in every patient.

Begin azathioprine monotherapy: Azathioprine may be selected when steroids are contraindicated or poorly tolerated, but corticosteroids are the generally recommended initial immune agent in the stated uncomplicated context.

Begin regularly scheduled IVIG maintenance: IVIG can be useful in selected severe or refractory MG, but is not the usual first immune step for stable isolated ocular disease inadequately controlled symptomatically.

Refer for nonthymomatous thymectomy as the initial immune intervention: Surgery can be considered in selected contexts, but the strongest randomized evidence is in generalized AChR-positive disease; it is not the routine initial immune approach for this ocular presentation.

questions.question: An untreated patient with generalized MG has marked dysphagia, a weak cough and declining respiratory reserve. Long-term corticosteroid therapy is planned. Which approach best addresses the early treatment risk?
options: Admit for monitoring and begin rapid high-dose corticosteroid induction without short-term rescue
Admit for airway monitoring and rapid IVIG or exchange therapy, introducing steroids with an appropriate monitored plan
Begin azathioprine with a gradual outpatient prednisone escalation
Increase pyridostigmine with a brief monitored observation period
questions.explanation:
Corticosteroid Initiation in Significant Bulbar MG

Correct answer: Admit for airway monitoring and rapid IVIG or exchange therapy, introducing steroids with an appropriate monitored plan

Initial Worsening Is Clinically Important

**Corticosteroids can transiently exacerbate myasthenic weakness**, particularly when substantial bulbar or generalized disease is present. This risk does not negate their long-term immune benefit.

Assess secretion handling, swallowing, cough and ventilation before choosing the starting setting and regimen. A normal oxygen saturation does not establish adequate ventilatory reserve.

Stable mild disease may be treated through gradual outpatient escalation, whereas severe or rapidly evolving bulbar/respiratory involvement needs a monitored inpatient approach.

Bridge the Delay in Immune Control

**IVIG or plasma exchange provides a faster short-term effect** and may be given before or alongside carefully timed steroid introduction. In selected high-risk cases, allow rescue therapy to begin working before escalating steroids.

Choice depends on hemodynamics, access, renal and thrombotic risks, infection and local expertise. Intubation decisions remain clinical and should not wait for an immunotherapy response.

Plan the longer course with objective functional assessment and steroid toxicity prevention. Glucose, BP, mood, bone and infection risks require monitoring. Neither a brief improvement after pyridostigmine nor initiation of a steroid-sparing agent removes the need for serial bulbar and respiratory review during early treatment.

Admit for monitoring and begin rapid high-dose corticosteroid induction without short-term rescue: Steroids may be introduced under monitoring, but significant bulbar and declining respiratory reserve make rapid IVIG/exchange and attention to initial steroid worsening particularly appropriate.

Begin azathioprine with a gradual outpatient prednisone escalation: This can be part of longer-term treatment for stable disease, but delayed drug onset and the supplied airway-related findings make an outpatient plan unsuitable now.

Increase pyridostigmine with a brief monitored observation period: Symptomatic adjustment can help mild weakness, but cannot provide sufficient immune control for this high-risk trajectory and may increase secretion burden.

questions.question: A patient starting azathioprine for steroid-dependent MG has normal TPMT and NUDT15 results. Which monitoring plan remains appropriate?
options: Serial CBC with platelets and liver tests, with closer checks during initiation and dose changes
Serial liver tests with symptom-triggered blood counts
Serial thiopurine metabolites with symptom-triggered blood counts
CBC and liver tests only after the first six months of treatment
questions.explanation:
Azathioprine and Pharmacogenetic Safety

Correct answer: Serial CBC with platelets and liver tests, with closer checks during initiation and dose changes

Delayed Steroid-Sparing Benefit

**Azathioprine is a thiopurine immunosuppressant** used in selected MG patients needing longer-term steroid reduction. Clinical benefit commonly takes months, so it is not rescue treatment for crisis.

A common adult approach begins at ==50 mg/day== and titrates toward approximately ==2–3 mg/kg/day== if appropriate and tolerated. Adjust to the patient, pharmacogenetic result, interactions and laboratory trends.

Obtain baseline CBC, liver and renal assessment and use TPMT/NUDT15 information according to local practice. Reduced activity can require substantial dose adjustment or an alternative agent.

Genotyping Does Not Replace Surveillance

**Monitor marrow and hepatic toxicity even with normal tested genotypes.** The US label describes CBC checks weekly during month one, twice monthly during months two and three, then monthly or more often when clinically needed.

Check the local specialty protocol for liver-test timing and subsequent stable monitoring. Explain infection precautions and the importance of reporting bruising, fever or other toxicity symptoms.

Allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit a pathway of thiopurine inactivation and can cause serious toxicity with usual azathioprine dosing. Reconcile medications before initiation and dose changes; any deliberate combination requires specialist dose management rather than an automatic standard regimen. Review long-term malignancy/skin risks and reproductive plans in shared decisions.

Serial liver tests with symptom-triggered blood counts: Liver monitoring is important, but cytopenias can precede symptoms; normal tested genotypes do not make scheduled CBC surveillance unnecessary.

Serial thiopurine metabolites with symptom-triggered blood counts: Metabolites answer selected exposure questions, but cannot substitute for direct scheduled monitoring of blood counts and hepatic toxicity.

CBC and liver tests only after the first six months of treatment: Stable long-term intervals may be extended under local protocols, but early initiation and titration need closer checks because serious toxicity can develop before six months.

questions.question: Which outcome is supported by MGTX for a patient matching its nonthymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG population?
options: Improved clinical control with reduced prednisone requirements versus prednisone alone
Superiority to rituximab as initial steroid-sparing therapy
Equivalent benefit across AChR-positive and MuSK-positive subgroups
Rapid prevention of intubation during an established crisis
questions.explanation:
Thymectomy Evidence in Nonthymomatous MG

Correct answer: Improved clinical control with reduced prednisone requirements versus prednisone alone

What MGTX Tested

**MGTX compared thymectomy plus prednisone with prednisone alone** in nonthymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG. Its enrolled population was aged 18–65 years, with disease duration under five years and MGFA II–IV disease.

The study demonstrated improved clinical measures and reduced steroid requirements over follow-up. It did not test surgery as an acute rescue, nor establish benefit for every antibody subgroup or phenotype.

Distinguish trial eligibility from the strength of a recommendation for an individual age group. The 2020 international update particularly supported early consideration in ages 18–50.

Apply Evidence to an Elective Decision

**The 2025 ABN update recommends early thymectomy below 50 years in AChR MG and consideration at 50–65**, integrating comorbidity, disease course and patient preference.

Assess operative and respiratory risk and optimize MG before surgery. Discuss surgical approach and expertise without assuming every minimally invasive technique has identical randomized comparative evidence.

A thymoma requires tumor-directed multidisciplinary assessment regardless of whether the patient matches the nonthymomatous trial population. Continue postoperative clinical and medication review; thymectomy does not guarantee remission or allow immediate unmonitored withdrawal of immune treatment.

Superiority to rituximab as initial steroid-sparing therapy: MGTX compared thymectomy plus prednisone with prednisone alone, not rituximab; its results cannot establish that active-treatment comparison.

Equivalent benefit across AChR-positive and MuSK-positive subgroups: The trial addressed AChR-positive generalized disease; MuSK patients were not an equivalent randomized subgroup from which to infer the same benefit.

Rapid prevention of intubation during an established crisis: MGTX studied longer-term outcomes rather than crisis rescue; acute airway and rapid immune treatment decisions must precede elective surgical considerations.

MGTX randomized trial of thymectomy, 2016 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1602489

International consensus guidance for MG: 2020 update, published 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000011124

ABN autoimmune MG management guideline, 2025 update — https://doi.org/10.1136/pn-2025-004655

questions.question: A patient with MuSK-positive generalized MG continues to have important bulbar weakness despite initial corticosteroid treatment and tolerates pyridostigmine poorly. After stabilization, which longer-term strategy has particular consensus support for this subgroup?
options: Nonthymomatous thymectomy
Rituximab
Ravulizumab
Azathioprine alone with no bridging plan
questions.explanation:
Early Rituximab Consideration in MuSK MG

Correct answer: Rituximab

A Subgroup-Specific Immune Strategy

**Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells**, reducing an important source of ongoing antibody-producing immune activity. It is not an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or an immediate substitute for airway support.

The 2020 international update supports early consideration in MuSK MG with an unsatisfactory response to initial immunotherapy; later specialty guidance also emphasizes its early role in this phenotype.

The evidence base includes observational experience and differs from the randomized evidence for some newer therapies. Do not describe a guaranteed response, identical benefit across all antibody groups or a universal licensed MG indication.

Screen and Follow Beyond the Infusion

**Assess hepatitis B with HBsAg and anti-HBc**, baseline immunoglobulins, infection history, vaccination needs and relevant laboratory data. Prior resolved HBV infection can still confer reactivation risk.

Coordinate antiviral prevention and follow-up with an experienced service when indicated. Monitor infusion reactions, infections and clinically meaningful hypogammaglobulinemia; vaccination planning is best addressed before B-cell depletion where feasible.

Specialist regimens vary, including 1 g IV on days 1 and 15 or alternative schedules; follow the selected protocol rather than assuming one schedule applies to every autoimmune condition. Assess objective bulbar, respiratory and functional outcomes over time, and provide rapid rescue separately when severe weakness cannot wait for longer-term immune control.

Nonthymomatous thymectomy: Thymectomy has specific tumor and AChR-generalized evidence-based roles, but does not have the same supported immune benefit in MuSK disease.

Ravulizumab: Ravulizumab blocks C5 and has an adult AChR-positive generalized MG indication; predominant MuSK IgG4 biology and subgroup evidence make this a different therapeutic context.

Azathioprine alone with no bridging plan: Azathioprine is a legitimate steroid-sparing option in MG, but its delayed onset is a limitation in persistent important bulbar disease; early rituximab has particular consensus support in MuSK MG.

questions.question: An adult with AChR-positive generalized MG is scheduled to begin ravulizumab. Treatment can safely wait while preventive measures are arranged. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Update MenACWY and MenB vaccination before treatment and counsel about persistent infection risk
Update MenACWY vaccination and use routine boosters
Update MenB vaccination and use routine boosters
Use antibacterial prophylaxis with vaccination deferred until treatment completion
questions.explanation:
Meningococcal Risk With C5 Inhibition

Correct answer: Update MenACWY and MenB vaccination before treatment and counsel about persistent infection risk

Mechanism Creates a Specific Infection Risk

**Ravulizumab blocks terminal complement C5**, reducing an important effector mechanism in AChR-antibody MG. The same blockade impairs defense against invasive meningococcal infection.

The 2026 US MG indication is adult AChR-positive generalized disease. Do not transfer this indication automatically to isolated ocular or MuSK-positive disease.

Meningococcal illness can develop despite vaccination or prophylaxis. Explain fever, headache, neck stiffness, rash and systemic illness as reasons for immediate medical assessment rather than reassurance from a vaccine history.

Vaccination and Urgent-Start Planning

**Complete or update MenACWY and MenB vaccination ideally at least two weeks before treatment**, following the current risk-based schedule and boosters.

If delaying treatment is clinically unsafe, follow the product label for prompt vaccination and antibacterial prophylaxis. Additional prophylaxis during ongoing treatment can be considered according to specialist and local guidance.

Check for unresolved serious meningococcal infection before initiation and maintain a clear emergency pathway. Assess clinical response, infection and other adverse effects over time. Complement inhibition is disease-directed treatment, but acute airway support and rapid rescue decisions remain separate; an evolving crisis must not wait for elective preventive scheduling.

Update MenACWY vaccination and use routine boosters: MenACWY vaccination is necessary, but alone leaves out the recommended MenB component for complement-inhibitor recipients.

Update MenB vaccination and use routine boosters: MenB vaccination is necessary, but alone does not cover the other serogroups addressed by MenACWY; both categories are recommended.

Use antibacterial prophylaxis with vaccination deferred until treatment completion: Urgent-start prophylaxis can be needed when treatment cannot wait, but does not justify postponing indicated vaccines until the entire course ends when preventive planning is feasible.

questions.question: Which mechanism explains the effect of FcRn blockers such as rozanolixizumab in autoimmune generalized MG?
options: Inhibition of cleavage of complement C5
Depletion of CD20-positive B cells
Reduced recycling and increased degradation of circulating IgG
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the motor end plate
questions.explanation:
FcRn Blockade and IgG Recycling

Correct answer: Reduced recycling and increased degradation of circulating IgG

Lower IgG Through a Salvage Pathway

**FcRn normally rescues IgG from intracellular degradation.** Blocking this receptor lowers circulating IgG, including pathogenic autoantibodies, without directly correcting every cause of weakness.

The mechanism differs from B-cell depletion, terminal complement blockade and symptomatic acetylcholinesterase inhibition. Drugs sharing an MG indication are therefore not interchangeable in mechanism or monitoring.

Antibody subgroup, indication, route and treatment-cycle schedule are product specific. Evidence for one FcRn drug cannot automatically be used as the approved indication or exact regimen of another.

Infection, Vaccines and Treatment Assessment

**Assess active infection and vaccination needs** before treatment. Because IgG falls transiently, live vaccines are generally not recommended during the treatment period specified by the product instructions.

Monitor hypersensitivity, infection and relevant formulation-specific adverse effects. Rozanolixizumab commonly causes headache, and aseptic meningitis is an important recognized warning; a severe headache still requires clinical evaluation for competing causes.

Use objective symptoms and function to determine response and subsequent treatment planning. A biochemical IgG decline is not itself proof that every symptom is myasthenic or that the patient has achieved remission. Concomitant immune therapies and immunoglobulin exposure require specialist coordination rather than unplanned stacking of treatments with overlapping effects.

Inhibition of cleavage of complement C5: Terminal complement inhibitors act downstream on complement-mediated injury; their mechanism and meningococcal precautions differ from FcRn-mediated IgG reduction.

Depletion of CD20-positive B cells: This describes rituximab and related B-cell therapies; FcRn blockade alters IgG handling rather than directly depleting CD20-positive cells.

Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the motor end plate: Pyridostigmine provides symptomatic synaptic benefit by slowing acetylcholine breakdown; it does not lower pathogenic IgG through altered recycling.

questions.question: An 82-kg adult with MuSK-positive generalized MG is prescribed rozanolixizumab under its US label. Which regimen matches the cited prescribing information?
options: 420 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for six weeks
560 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for six weeks
840 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for six weeks
560 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for four weeks
questions.explanation:
Rozanolixizumab Indication and Cycle

Correct answer: 560 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for six weeks

Read the Antibody and Weight Requirements

**The cited US RYSTIGGO label includes adult generalized MG with AChR or MuSK antibodies.** This is a product-specific indication rather than a statement that every targeted MG drug covers both groups.

The 82-kg patient falls in the ==50 to under 100 kg== band and receives ==560 mg weekly for six weeks==. Administration is by subcutaneous infusion using the specified equipment and preparation procedure.

The label’s other bands are 420 mg below 50 kg and 840 mg at 100 kg or above. Do not substitute an infusion dose from a different weight group or convert the regimen to an unrelated fixed four-dose cycle.

Plan Subsequent Cycles Clinically

**Further cycles depend on clinical evaluation.** In the cited label, the safety of starting another cycle sooner than 63 days after the previous cycle began has not been established.

Review infection and age-appropriate immunizations before a new cycle, with attention to the live-vaccine restriction during treatment. Monitor headache, hypersensitivity and possible aseptic meningitis.

Assess MG symptoms, function and respiratory/bulbar status rather than scheduling repeat cycles from the antibody titer alone. The US label defines the example here; local approval, availability and instructions must be checked separately. A routine outpatient cycle is not a substitute for airway management in an acute crisis.

420 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for six weeks: This dose corresponds to the under-50-kg weight band in the cited label; the 82-kg patient belongs to the 50-to-under-100-kg group.

840 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for six weeks: This dose corresponds to patients weighing at least 100 kg, rather than the supplied 82-kg weight.

560 mg by subcutaneous infusion once weekly for four weeks: The weight-band dose is correct, but the labeled rozanolixizumab cycle contains six weekly doses; a different FcRn product’s cycle should not be copied.

US RYSTIGGO/rozanolixizumab prescribing information — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/761286s007lbl.pdf

questions.question: A term infant develops hypotonia, a weak cry and poor sucking during the first two days after birth. The mother has autoimmune MG that was clinically well controlled during pregnancy. Which mechanism best explains the suspected neonatal syndrome?
options: Transplacental transfer of maternal pathogenic IgG
An inherited congenital myasthenic syndrome
A congenital structural myopathy
A congenital myotonic dystrophy mechanism
questions.explanation:
Transient Neonatal Myasthenia

Correct answer: Transplacental transfer of maternal pathogenic IgG

Passive Autoimmunity Can Occur Despite Maternal Control

**Maternal IgG crosses the placenta** and can temporarily impair neonatal neuromuscular transmission. Good maternal symptom control does not exclude neonatal weakness.

Poor feeding, weak cry, hypotonia and respiratory difficulty require prompt neonatal assessment. Evaluate sepsis, metabolic disease, central illness and congenital neuromuscular disorders as competing or additional causes.

Provide feeding and respiratory support as needed; selected infants receive specialist-directed acetylcholinesterase inhibition. The usual course improves over weeks as maternal antibodies disappear.

Plan Pregnancy and Delivery Prospectively

**Coordinate neurology, obstetrics, anesthesia and neonatal care.** Review medications before conception, maintain disease control and arrange neonatal observation after delivery.

Oral pyridostigmine and appropriately selected corticosteroid treatment can be used under supervision. Mycophenolate and methotrexate are incompatible with pregnancy; withdrawal, substitution and contraception/washout planning require a specialist plan rather than abrupt unmonitored cessation.

Magnesium sulfate can significantly worsen transmission in MG and should not be used as an automatic obstetric default; severe preeclampsia/eclampsia needs urgent individualized multidisciplinary management. Vaginal delivery is often feasible, with support if skeletal-muscle fatigue limits the second stage. Monitor maternal symptoms postpartum as well as during gestation.

An inherited congenital myasthenic syndrome: CMS can cause neonatal hypotonia and feeding/respiratory weakness, but maternal autoimmune MG strongly raises passive antibody-mediated neonatal disease; persistence or atypical findings warrants genetic reassessment.

A congenital structural myopathy: Congenital myopathy is an important neonatal weakness differential, but the maternal autoimmune history and early transient-transmission context particularly support transferred antibodies.

A congenital myotonic dystrophy mechanism: Congenital DM1 can cause severe neonatal hypotonia, but usually reflects maternal DMPK disease rather than maternal autoimmune MG; it has a different inherited mechanism and course.

International consensus guidance for MG, 2016: short-term rescue and steroid precautions — https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000002790

AGG recommendations for MG in pregnancy, 2021 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8654508/

questions.question: A patient with MG and a respiratory infection reports little change in limb strength but now cannot finish sentences, coughs weakly and repeatedly chokes on saliva. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. What is the best next step?
options: Outpatient prednisone escalation with early telephone review
Ward admission for antibiotics with intermittent saturation checks
A trial of increased oral pyridostigmine before deciding the monitoring setting
Urgent monitored airway/ventilation assessment and critical-care escalation
questions.explanation:
Recognizing Impending Myasthenic Crisis

Correct answer: Urgent monitored airway/ventilation assessment and critical-care escalation

Bulbar Failure Can Precede Obvious Desaturation

**Impending crisis is a clinical trajectory**, not a pulse-oximetry threshold. Inability to manage saliva, weak cough, dysarthria and progressive breathlessness can signal danger before severe hypoxemia.

Assess swallowing, secretion clearance, work of breathing, neck strength and ability to speak. Serial respiratory mechanics complement this examination rather than replacing it.

Limited limb weakness does not establish safety. Bulbar and respiratory muscles can be disproportionately affected, particularly in some antibody phenotypes.

Protect the Airway While Treating the Trigger

**Arrange monitored care and an anticipatory airway plan**, with neurology, critical care and experienced airway input. Avoid oral intake when swallowing is unsafe and manage aspiration and secretions.

Look for infection, medication changes, missed therapy, surgery or other precipitating stress. Treat the cause while planning rapid MG therapy such as IVIG or exchange when indicated.

Noninvasive ventilation is suitable only in selected patients who can protect the airway and clear secretions, with close monitoring and rapid access to intubation. Do not let a trial delay intubation in worsening bulbar failure. Completion of a diagnostic test or the onset of an immune-treatment effect must not become a prerequisite for life-saving respiratory support.

Outpatient prednisone escalation with early telephone review: This approach can fit stable disease under a planned protocol, but significant bulbar and respiratory warning features require monitored assessment and possible rescue therapy now.

Ward admission for antibiotics with intermittent saturation checks: Antibiotics address the trigger, but intermittent saturation monitoring alone does not capture rapidly evolving ventilatory or secretion failure; higher-acuity airway assessment is warranted.

A trial of increased oral pyridostigmine before deciding the monitoring setting: Symptomatic adjustment can help stable weakness, but choking on saliva and weak cough require urgent airway assessment before waiting to judge an oral drug response.

MGFA emergency management guidance — https://myasthenia.org/understanding-mg/learn-more-about-mg-treatments/mg-brochures/emergency-management-for-first-responders/

questions.question: During monitored treatment of MG, vital capacity falls from 28 to 17 mL/kg over four hours. The patient develops paradoxical breathing and cannot clear secretions; oxygen saturation remains 97%. Which respiratory strategy is most appropriate?
options: High-flow nasal oxygen with serial saturation-guided escalation
A closely observed noninvasive ventilation trial as the first airway strategy
Timely endotracheal intubation with continued immune and supportive treatment
A short delay for another respiratory-mechanics measurement before intervention
questions.explanation:
Respiratory Mechanics and Airway Timing

Correct answer: Timely endotracheal intubation with continued immune and supportive treatment

Use Numbers as Warning Signals

**VC around or below ==20 mL/kg==** and inspiratory pressure weaker than about −30 cm H2O are concerning in the appropriate setting. A less negative inspiratory pressure means weaker force.

These are warning values rather than mandatory universal intubation cutoffs. Bulbar dysfunction, poor seal, effort and measurement technique affect reliability.

Trend, work of breathing, cough, aspiration risk and blood gases determine urgency. Hypercapnia can indicate advanced ventilatory compromise and should not be awaited before acting.

Avoid an Emergency Airway After Exhaustion

**Rapidly declining reserve with failed secretion clearance** favors elective controlled airway management over delayed rescue after collapse. In this stem, clinical deterioration independently reinforces the concerning VC.

Selected nonhypercapnic patients with effective airway protection may benefit from closely supervised noninvasive support; frequent reassessment and an intubation plan remain essential.

Ventilation supports the patient while immune treatment takes effect. Provide aspiration management, infection treatment, nutrition, thrombosis prevention and rehabilitation as appropriate. Extubation later requires improvement in cough, secretion handling and overall respiratory performance, not merely one satisfactory VC measurement.

High-flow nasal oxygen with serial saturation-guided escalation: High-flow oxygen can help selected hypoxemic disorders, but does not reliably correct neuromuscular ventilation failure or protect this secretion-compromised airway.

A closely observed noninvasive ventilation trial as the first airway strategy: Noninvasive support can be appropriate when airway protection and secretion clearance are effective; their failure here, with rapidly declining reserve, favors intubation.

A short delay for another respiratory-mechanics measurement before intervention: Repeating a questionable isolated measurement is reasonable, but the reproducible rapid decline plus paradoxical breathing and secretion failure already supplies independent evidence to act.

questions.question: An adult has been stabilized in monitored care for severe generalized MG deterioration. Which pair consists of established rapid immune-treatment alternatives for this setting?
options: Azathioprine or mycophenolate
IVIG or plasma exchange
Rituximab or elective thymectomy
Pyridostigmine or amifampridine
questions.explanation:
Rapid Immune Therapy in Severe Exacerbation

Correct answer: IVIG or plasma exchange

Choose a Short-Term Bridge

**IVIG and plasma exchange are established short-term therapies** for significant generalized exacerbation, crisis and selected perioperative or steroid-initiation situations.

A common IVIG rescue course totals ==2 g/kg over 2–5 days==, although dose selection and local guidance vary. Assess thrombotic, renal, hemolytic and volume-related risks.

Exchange commonly uses approximately four to five procedures, with the exact schedule individualized. Consider access, hemodynamic tolerance, anticoagulation, calcium and infection risks.

Match the Modality to the Patient

**Exchange may act faster and can be particularly useful in MuSK disease**, but this does not mean one modality is always best for every patient. Availability and comorbidity materially affect the choice.

Continue respiratory and bulbar support independently of immune-treatment completion. Failure to improve immediately should prompt review of timing, complications, diagnosis and adequacy rather than automatic repetitive courses.

Introduce or adjust sustained immune therapy with attention to initial steroid worsening. Rapid therapy is a bridge and does not by itself establish a long-term maintenance plan. Document objective strength, swallowing, ventilation and functional response so later decisions rest on clinical benefit rather than an assumed pharmacologic effect.

Azathioprine or mycophenolate: Both have steroid-sparing maintenance roles, but their delayed clinical effect prevents them from substituting for rapid rescue during severe exacerbation.

Rituximab or elective thymectomy: Both can have important disease-modifying roles in selected MG populations, but neither is the standard immediate rescue alternative to IVIG or exchange in this acute setting.

Pyridostigmine or amifampridine: These alter transmission symptomatically, with amifampridine mainly used in LEMS; they do not constitute the established rapid immune-treatment pair for severe autoimmune MG.

questions.question: Which antibiotic carries a specific US boxed warning about exacerbating myasthenia gravis and should generally be avoided in a patient with known MG when an effective safer alternative is available?
options: Ciprofloxacin
Amoxicillin–clavulanate
Cefuroxime
Doxycycline
questions.explanation:
Fluoroquinolones and MG Worsening

Correct answer: Ciprofloxacin

Medication Review During Deterioration

**Fluoroquinolones can impair neuromuscular transmission** and have a boxed warning for exacerbation in known MG. Review newly introduced drugs whenever weakness worsens.

Macrolides, aminoglycosides and intravenous magnesium are other important caution categories, although the evidence, risk and clinical necessity differ among exposures.

Sedatives, opioids and drugs with neuromuscular-blocking effects can further compromise ventilation or airway safety in a weak patient. The medication list should include nonprescription products and recent procedures.

Treat Infection Without Creating Another Hazard

**Infection itself can precipitate exacerbation or crisis.** Avoid delaying necessary antimicrobial treatment while debating medication risk; choose an effective lower-risk agent when feasible.

Base therapy on the infection source, culture, severity, allergies, renal function and local resistance. A caution list is not proof that every reported association is an absolute contraindication.

If a higher-risk drug is essential and alternatives are unsuitable, use an informed specialist plan with appropriate monitoring. Document timing, objective weakness and competing triggers rather than assuming causality from coincidence alone. New dysphagia, weak cough or respiratory decline requires urgent clinical assessment, not simply discontinuing a drug and waiting at home.

Amoxicillin–clavulanate: This can be an appropriate infection-directed option and lacks the fluoroquinolone-specific boxed MG warning; selection still depends on allergy, organism and local susceptibility.

Cefuroxime: A cephalosporin may be appropriate for selected infections and does not share the fluoroquinolone boxed MG warning; the infection site and microbiology remain essential.

Doxycycline: Doxycycline can be selected for suitable infections and does not carry the fluoroquinolone-specific boxed MG warning; no antibiotic choice should be made without considering indication and individual tolerability.

questions.question: A patient intubated for myasthenic crisis is receiving IVIG and has copious airway secretions while taking regular pyridostigmine. Which medication adjustment is generally appropriate during this phase?
options: Increase pyridostigmine as the main strategy to accelerate ventilator liberation
Continue the same dose and add an antimuscarinic for secretions
Temporarily withhold or reduce pyridostigmine, with planned reassessment before reintroduction
Substitute continuous intravenous pyridostigmine during the intubated period
questions.explanation:
Pyridostigmine During Intubated Crisis

Correct answer: Temporarily withhold or reduce pyridostigmine, with planned reassessment before reintroduction

Separate Symptom Treatment From Rescue

**Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors increase acetylcholine and secretions.** During intubated crisis, temporary reduction or withholding commonly simplifies secretion management and avoids dose-related cholinergic effects.

This does not mean pyridostigmine caused every crisis. Infection, inadequate disease control and other triggers remain important, and airway support plus rapid immune treatment continue.

Consult the neuromuscular and intensive-care teams rather than applying an unqualified medication-stop rule to every nonintubated patient with mild symptoms.

Reintroduce According to Clinical Recovery

**Restart symptomatic treatment when strength and airway function improve**, often near the extubation period, using an individualized dose and assessment of secretion burden.

Extubation readiness depends on cough, secretion handling, bulbar function, respiratory performance and the broader clinical course. Neither a pyridostigmine dose nor a single lung-volume measurement establishes readiness.

Monitor bradycardia, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, fasciculation and excess salivation when restarting or titrating. Renal impairment can increase exposure and may require adjustment. A new decline after dosing should trigger reassessment for both toxicity and ongoing disease; routine intravenous diagnostic challenge is not necessary to resolve every uncertain episode.

Increase pyridostigmine as the main strategy to accelerate ventilator liberation: Symptomatic benefit may help later recovery, but escalation during a secretion-heavy intubated phase can worsen cholinergic burden and does not replace immune rescue.

Continue the same dose and add an antimuscarinic for secretions: An antimuscarinic can manage selected side effects in stable patients, but the intubated crisis setting warrants reconsidering pyridostigmine itself rather than automatically masking excess secretions.

Substitute continuous intravenous pyridostigmine during the intubated period: Intravenous cholinesterase inhibition has selected specialist uses but adds secretion and arrhythmic concerns and is not the routine solution to this presentation.

questions.question: After repeatedly increasing pyridostigmine, a patient develops worsening weakness accompanied by marked salivation, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, miosis, fasciculation and bradycardia. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Excess acetylcholinesterase inhibition causing cholinergic toxicity
Isolated autoimmune MG exacerbation
Steroid-induced myopathy
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
questions.explanation:
Cholinergic Toxicity After Dose Escalation

Correct answer: Excess acetylcholinesterase inhibition causing cholinergic toxicity

Muscarinic and Nicotinic Effects Coexist

**Excess acetylcholine can paradoxically worsen strength** while producing muscarinic salivation, bronchial secretions, diarrhea, cramping, miosis and bradycardia.

Fasciculation and weakness reflect nicotinic effects. Weakness alone cannot distinguish toxicity from MG activity; exposure history and the accompanying findings are crucial.

Cholinergic crisis is uncommon in modern routine MG care, but clinically important toxicity must still be considered after excess dosing or impaired clearance.

Stabilize Before Assigning the Entire Cause

**Assess airway and ventilation urgently**, with monitored supportive care and withholding the offending exposure. Review renal function, dosing errors, overlapping preparations and other causes of deterioration.

Atropine can treat significant muscarinic manifestations under appropriate supervision, but does not reverse nicotinic weakness. Clearing secretions pharmacologically does not establish restoration of respiratory muscle function.

Do not give additional pyridostigmine reflexively or use a hazardous edrophonium challenge as the routine arbiter in respiratory distress. Autoimmune exacerbation or infection can coexist, so continue clinical reassessment and treat the supported underlying processes. Reintroduce an appropriate symptomatic regimen only after stabilization and a clear medication plan.

Isolated autoimmune MG exacerbation: Autoimmune worsening can cause weakness and respiratory compromise, but the clustered muscarinic signs and fasciculation after dose escalation strongly suggest an additional toxic cholinergic mechanism.

Steroid-induced myopathy: Steroid myopathy usually causes relatively painless proximal weakness without this acute secretory, gastrointestinal, pupillary and bradycardic syndrome linked to pyridostigmine escalation.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: LEMS can cause proximal weakness and autonomic symptoms, but often dry mouth rather than cholinergic excess, and does not explain this dose-linked muscarinic cluster.

questions.question: An older smoker has proximal leg weakness, dry mouth and depressed reflexes that briefly improve after contraction. Baseline CMAP is low and increases by 160% immediately after brief maximal exercise. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
AChR-positive generalized myasthenia gravis
Motor-predominant CIDP
Inclusion body myositis
questions.explanation:
Presynaptic Facilitation in LEMS

Correct answer: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome

Reduced Release With Exercise-Related Compensation

**LEMS commonly involves antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels**, reducing acetylcholine release. Calcium accumulation during activation can transiently improve release and strength.

Typical clues are proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth and reduced tendon reflexes that facilitate after activation. Ocular and bulbar symptoms can occur, so their presence does not automatically establish MG.

Electrodiagnostics combine low baseline motor responses, possible low-frequency decrement and substantial postexercise or high-frequency increment. Interpret percentages together with the actual baseline response and recording quality.

Thresholds and Next Decisions

**An increment exceeding ==100%== is the classic highly supportive pattern**; a threshold around ==60%== can improve sensitivity under validated protocols. A technically sound ==160%== increment fits either approach.

Brief maximal exercise and immediate recording matter; delayed sampling can miss facilitation. Calcium-channel antibodies support a concordant syndrome but should not replace clinical and electrophysiological interpretation.

Assess for associated small-cell lung cancer and provide symptomatic treatment, commonly amifampridine when suitable. Autoimmune nonparaneoplastic disease also occurs. Address mobility, falls and autonomic symptoms while the cancer investigation proceeds rather than treating this as an isolated laboratory finding.

Feature | MG | LEMS

Common weakness emphasis | Ocular/bulbar, neck and proximal limbs | Proximal legs often prominent

Reflexes | Usually preserved | Often reduced with postactivation facilitation

Autonomic clues | Not a defining feature | Dry mouth and other autonomic symptoms

Electrophysiology | Low-frequency decrement; increased jitter | Low resting CMAP; large postexercise increment

Common antibody target | AChR or MuSK | P/Q-type calcium channel

AChR-positive generalized myasthenia gravis: MG can cause proximal weakness and low-frequency decrement, but autonomic symptoms, depressed facilitating reflexes and a large postexercise increment favor presynaptic LEMS.

Motor-predominant CIDP: CIDP can produce weakness and areflexia, but requires an appropriate demyelinating pattern rather than this striking exercise-related increment and autonomic phenotype.

Inclusion body myositis: IBM can cause quadriceps weakness in older adults, but usually has a chronic characteristic muscle pattern without this presynaptic electrodiagnostic facilitation or autonomic syndrome.

bullets.text: **LEMS commonly involves antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels**, reducing acetylcholine release. Calcium accumulation during activation can transiently improve release and strength.
children: Typical clues are proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth and reduced tendon reflexes that facilitate after activation. Ocular and bulbar symptoms can occur, so their presence does not automatically establish MG.

Electrodiagnostics combine low baseline motor responses, possible low-frequency decrement and substantial postexercise or high-frequency increment. Interpret percentages together with the actual baseline response and recording quality.

bullets.text: **An increment exceeding ==100%== is the classic highly supportive pattern**; a threshold around ==60%== can improve sensitivity under validated protocols. A technically sound ==160%== increment fits either approach.
children: Brief maximal exercise and immediate recording matter; delayed sampling can miss facilitation. Calcium-channel antibodies support a concordant syndrome but should not replace clinical and electrophysiological interpretation.

Assess for associated small-cell lung cancer and provide symptomatic treatment, commonly amifampridine when suitable. Autoimmune nonparaneoplastic disease also occurs. Address mobility, falls and autonomic symptoms while the cancer investigation proceeds rather than treating this as an isolated laboratory finding.

questions.question: A 61-year-old smoker has confirmed LEMS. Initial thoracic CT shows no malignancy. Which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Defer repeat screening until five years after the initial CT
Discharge from cancer surveillance after the negative initial CT
Repeat screening only if new chest symptoms develop
Repeat risk-directed screening at approximately 3–6-month intervals for at least two years
questions.explanation:
Cancer Surveillance After Negative Initial LEMS Imaging

Correct answer: Repeat risk-directed screening at approximately 3–6-month intervals for at least two years

Neurologic Disease May Precede Cancer Detection

**Small-cell lung cancer is the key associated malignancy.** Age, smoking history, weight loss and other clinical features modify risk, but do not replace a proper initial evaluation.

Thoracic CT is central to the search. Additional imaging, including FDG-PET in selected circumstances, depends on residual suspicion and specialist evaluation.

A negative result is a time-specific observation, not proof that cancer will never emerge. Explain the surveillance plan clearly so follow-up is not lost after symptomatic improvement.

A Scheduled, Risk-Adjusted Search

**Common specialty recommendations repeat screening every 3–6 months for at least two years**, with the exact duration and intensity individualized to risk and findings.

Reassess sooner for new systemic or respiratory symptoms, weight loss or suspicious imaging. Risk scores can help organize surveillance but should not override concerning clinical evidence.

If cancer is identified, coordinate tissue diagnosis, staging and oncologic treatment with neurologic care. Continue symptomatic and, where needed, immune treatment for LEMS; improvement in strength does not establish absence of cancer. Support smoking cessation and function while avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures without a clinical indication.

Defer repeat screening until five years after the initial CT: A long interval misses the period when an occult associated tumor may emerge after neurologic presentation; early risk-directed follow-up is more appropriate.

Discharge from cancer surveillance after the negative initial CT: One negative study can occur before a tumor becomes detectable; higher-risk LEMS warrants a scheduled surveillance pathway rather than closure.

Repeat screening only if new chest symptoms develop: Symptoms should trigger earlier investigation, but scheduled screening is important because small-cell lung cancer may remain clinically silent while becoming detectable.

questions.question: An adult with LEMS is being considered for amifampridine. Which history is a contraindication under the cited US FIRDAPSE label?
options: Known NAT2 poor-metabolizer status
Stable mild renal impairment
A prior seizure disorder
Paresthesias after an earlier dose
questions.explanation:
Amifampridine and Seizure History

Correct answer: A prior seizure disorder

Increase Presynaptic Release

**Amifampridine blocks potassium channels**, prolonging presynaptic depolarization and improving acetylcholine release. It provides symptomatic benefit in LEMS rather than treating an underlying malignancy.

The July 2025 US adult starting range is ==15–30 mg/day in 3–5 divided doses==. Titrate total daily dose by 5 mg every 3–4 days according to response and tolerability.

The cited adult limits are ==20 mg per dose== and ==100 mg/day==. Product and jurisdiction matter; older or non-US schedules should not be silently substituted for the specified label.

Assess Exposure and Seizure Risk

**A seizure history is a contraindication**, and seizures can also occur without prior epilepsy. Review medicines that lower seizure threshold and reassess promptly if a seizure occurs.

Renal or hepatic impairment and known NAT2 poor metabolism call for the lowest recommended initial daily dose. Follow specific renal guidance; the label does not provide an end-stage renal disease regimen.

Monitor adverse effects and practical strength/function. Pyridostigmine may be an adjunct in selected patients but adds cholinergic adverse-effect considerations. Treat associated cancer where present, and consider specialist immune therapy when symptomatic measures are insufficient; increasing the release-enhancing drug through toxicity is not a substitute for revisiting the whole disease strategy.

Known NAT2 poor-metabolizer status: Poor metabolism increases exposure and supports the lowest recommended starting dose with monitoring, rather than automatically prohibiting use.

Stable mild renal impairment: Renal impairment requires a lower initial dose and careful titration under the label; it is not the same categorical contraindication as a history of seizures.

Paresthesias after an earlier dose: Paresthesias are a recognized adverse effect that may affect tolerability and titration; they are not equivalent to the label’s seizure-history contraindication.

questions.question: A young adult has lifelong exertional limb-girdle weakness, negative autoimmune MG antibodies and biallelic pathogenic DOK7 variants. Pyridostigmine worsened symptoms. Which approach best fits this diagnosis?
options: Pyridostigmine dose escalation
Salbutamol or ephedrine through a specialist genotype-directed plan
Fluoxetine or quinidine as slow-channel-directed treatment
Corticosteroid induction followed by azathioprine
questions.explanation:
Genotype-Directed Congenital Myasthenia Treatment

Correct answer: Salbutamol or ephedrine through a specialist genotype-directed plan

Inherited Transmission Disease Can Present Late

**Congenital myasthenic syndromes** arise from diverse genetic defects of presynaptic, synaptic or postsynaptic transmission. Recognition in adulthood does not exclude an inherited disorder.

Early symptoms, family history, episodic apnea or an atypical limb-girdle phenotype can provide clues. Inheritance varies by subtype, so counseling should follow the actual molecular diagnosis.

Electrophysiology may show transmission failure, but that does not establish autoimmunity. Interpret a genetic result for pathogenicity and phenotype rather than treating every uncertain variant as a diagnosis.

The Same Symptomatic Drug Can Help or Harm

**DOK7-associated disease often benefits from beta-adrenergic agonist therapy** under specialist supervision. Salbutamol or ephedrine is chosen with attention to cardiac status, adverse effects and local availability.

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors can worsen DOK7, COLQ-related endplate enzyme deficiency and slow-channel disease. Other genotypes may respond well, illustrating why one inherited-NMJ regimen cannot be generalized.

Assess respiratory, swallowing, mobility and orthopedic needs directly. Treatment evidence is often based on small series rather than large trials, and response may take time. Genetic counseling, family evaluation and an emergency plan for decompensation complement medication; immunotherapy is not added merely because the symptoms resemble MG.

Pyridostigmine dose escalation: Pyridostigmine benefits several CMS subtypes, but DOK7 disease can fail to respond or worsen; the confirmed genotype and prior deterioration argue against escalation.

Fluoxetine or quinidine as slow-channel-directed treatment: These agents have selected roles in slow-channel CMS under specialist monitoring, but that channel-kinetic mechanism is not established by DOK7 variants.

Corticosteroid induction followed by azathioprine: This is an autoimmune-MG strategy rather than standard therapy for a confirmed inherited DOK7 transmission defect; seronegativity alone should not redirect the molecular diagnosis.

GeneReviews: congenital myasthenic syndromes overview — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1168/

Targeted therapies for congenital myasthenic syndromes: systematic review, 2019 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6436731/
