questions.question: Which disorder can cause progressive proximal muscle weakness despite repeatedly normal CK?
options: Duchenne muscular dystrophy early in the symptomatic course
Active anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy
Chronic glucocorticoid myopathy
Acute rhabdomyolysis after peak enzyme release
questions.explanation:
Normal CK Does Not Exclude Myopathy

Correct answer: Chronic glucocorticoid myopathy

A Marker of Injury Rather Than a Strength Meter

**CK reflects muscle membrane injury and enzyme release**, not the amount of weakness in a simple linear relationship. Some severe weakness occurs without substantial CK elevation.

Steroid myopathy, selected endocrine disorders, congenital myopathies and mitochondrial disease can have normal or modest values. Advanced loss of muscle bulk may also change the amount released.

Conversely, exercise, seizures, trauma and injections can raise CK without a primary chronic myopathy. Interpret the reference range and timing rather than treating one numerical result as a diagnosis.

Localize Before Selecting the Next Test

**Describe distribution, tempo and associated features**: proximal versus distal, symmetric versus asymmetric, ocular/bulbar involvement, sensory signs, reflexes and exertional or fasting triggers.

Review glucocorticoids, other myotoxic drugs, thyroid function, electrolytes, family history and systemic features. Use electrodiagnostics, targeted laboratory studies, muscle imaging or genetic assessment when indicated.

Normal CK and even a normal EMG do not exclude every muscle disorder. A highly specific inherited phenotype may warrant molecular testing, while suspected inflammation may need antibody, imaging and tissue integration. Progressive respiratory or swallowing weakness requires direct assessment regardless of enzyme results.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy early in the symptomatic course: Early symptomatic Duchenne disease generally has marked CK elevation; chronic glucocorticoid myopathy is a more characteristic normal-CK proximal disorder.

Active anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy: Active HMGCR IMNM usually produces substantial CK elevation with proximal weakness; normal values make it less characteristic than chronic steroid myopathy in this comparison.

Acute rhabdomyolysis after peak enzyme release: Rhabdomyolysis typically causes a substantial CK rise after muscle injury; repeatedly normal CK is not its expected biochemical pattern at the stated stage.

Continuum: a pattern-recognition approach to myopathy — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10564046/

questions.question: In weak proximal muscles, needle EMG shows short-duration, low-amplitude motor units with early recruitment. Sensory responses are preserved. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Reduced recruitment from an acute motor axonal lesion
Chronic neurogenic motor-unit remodeling
A myopathic motor-unit pattern
Reduced central activation without peripheral motor-unit change
questions.explanation:
Myopathic Recruitment on Needle EMG

Correct answer: A myopathic motor-unit pattern

Fewer Functioning Fibers Within a Motor Unit

**Loss or dysfunction of muscle fibers** can produce smaller, shorter motor-unit potentials. Recruitment occurs early because more units are needed to generate the requested force.

Sample an appropriate distribution and consider activation, disease stage and technical factors. Not every short unit is pathological, and end-stage or mixed disease can yield more complex patterns.

Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves indicate membrane irritability but are not unique to denervation or immune myositis. Some dystrophic, necrotizing and toxic processes are also irritable.

Use EMG to Refine, Not Replace, the Diagnosis

**Integrate CK, clinical distribution, exposures and systemic findings.** Sensory preservation supports a muscle/NMJ localization but does not distinguish those categories on its own.

Electrodiagnostics can identify a superimposed neuropathy, motor neuron disorder or transmission defect and can help choose a biopsy site when tissue is needed.

Selected myopathies have a normal or nondiagnostic EMG, particularly with limited sampling or fiber-selective pathology. A negative study should be weighed against the phenotype. When planning biopsy, avoid sampling recently needled tissue because procedure-related injury can obscure interpretation; use an appropriate contralateral muscle when disease symmetry permits.

Reduced recruitment from an acute motor axonal lesion: Acute axonal loss reduces the number of available motor units, whereas this early recruitment of small units better fits a myopathic pattern.

Chronic neurogenic motor-unit remodeling: Chronic reinnervation more commonly produces larger, longer-duration units and reduced recruitment; small short units with early recruitment point toward muscle-fiber dysfunction.

Reduced central activation without peripheral motor-unit change: Poor central activation may limit recruitment, but does not by itself explain the characteristic small short units with early recruitment described.

Electrodiagnostic evaluation of myopathies — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4435557/

children: Sample an appropriate distribution and consider activation, disease stage and technical factors. Not every short unit is pathological, and end-stage or mixed disease can yield more complex patterns.

Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves indicate membrane irritability but are not unique to denervation or immune myositis. Some dystrophic, necrotizing and toxic processes are also irritable.

sections.heading: Use EMG to Refine, Not Replace, the Diagnosis

bullets.text: **Integrate CK, clinical distribution, exposures and systemic findings.** Sensory preservation supports a muscle/NMJ localization but does not distinguish those categories on its own.
children: Electrodiagnostics can identify a superimposed neuropathy, motor neuron disorder or transmission defect and can help choose a biopsy site when tissue is needed.

Selected myopathies have a normal or nondiagnostic EMG, particularly with limited sampling or fiber-selective pathology. A negative study should be weighed against the phenotype. When planning biopsy, avoid sampling recently needled tissue because procedure-related injury can obscure interpretation; use an appropriate contralateral muscle when disease symmetry permits.

otherOptions.explanation: Acute axonal loss reduces the number of available motor units, whereas this early recruitment of small units better fits a myopathic pattern.
Chronic reinnervation more commonly produces larger, longer-duration units and reduced recruitment; small short units with early recruitment point toward muscle-fiber dysfunction.
Poor central activation may limit recruitment, but does not by itself explain the characteristic small short units with early recruitment described.

questions.question: A patient with suspected inflammatory myopathy needs muscle biopsy. MRI shows one moderately weak thigh muscle with edema and preserved bulk, while another is severely atrophic with extensive fatty replacement. Which site is preferable?
options: The recently needled portion of the moderately weak muscle
The severely atrophic muscle with maximal fatty replacement
A clinically strong muscle without MRI abnormalities
The affected, moderately weak muscle with preserved tissue, avoiding recent needle injury
questions.explanation:
Selecting a Muscle Biopsy Site

Correct answer: The affected, moderately weak muscle with preserved tissue, avoiding recent needle injury

Aim for Active, Interpretable Tissue

**Biopsy yield depends on selecting representative muscle**, often moderately weak and affected on imaging or examination, rather than normal tissue or end-stage destruction.

MRI can map edema, atrophy and fatty replacement and reveal a useful distribution. Edema is not specific for immune inflammation and may also follow exertion, denervation or injury.

Use the clinical question to determine whether tissue is needed at all. A secure genetic or antibody-defined diagnosis may change the value of biopsy, whereas unexplained disease may still require histology.

Plan the Procedure With the Laboratory

**Coordinate tissue handling and requested studies** before sampling. Histochemistry, immunostaining, biochemical or ultrastructural studies may require appropriate fresh/frozen material rather than routine fixation alone.

Avoid recent EMG sites and discuss treatment exposure, disease duration and distribution with the pathologist. Symmetric disease may allow biopsy of the contralateral counterpart to an electrodiagnostically abnormal muscle.

Interpret the report with the clinical phenotype and other tests. A nonspecific or negative sample does not automatically exclude a patchy inflammatory, metabolic or inherited disorder. Reassessment should identify whether sampling, timing or an alternative diagnosis explains discordance rather than simply repeating an invasive procedure without a new rationale.

The recently needled portion of the moderately weak muscle: EMG can identify an involved target, but biopsy directly through recent needle injury can introduce artifacts; use an appropriate nonneedled site or contralateral counterpart.

The severely atrophic muscle with maximal fatty replacement: A severely affected site may seem attractive, but end-stage destruction can yield nonspecific tissue with too little viable muscle for useful interpretation.

A clinically strong muscle without MRI abnormalities: A less affected muscle may be appropriate in some diffuse disorders, but an entirely normal site can miss patchy disease when a representative moderately affected site is available.

questions.question: An asymptomatic adult has CK twice the laboratory upper limit the day after an unusually strenuous gym session. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
options: Obtain muscle MRI and a broad genetic panel immediately
Repeat CK after a rest interval and review exercise, drugs and systemic contributors
Obtain needle EMG and proceed to biopsy if it is irritable
Stop follow-up because a normal examination excludes inherited muscle disease
questions.explanation:
Rechecking Incidental HyperCKemia

Correct answer: Repeat CK after a rest interval and review exercise, drugs and systemic contributors

Establish That the Finding Persists

**CK varies with activity and reference population.** Repeat after avoiding strenuous activity, commonly for about seven days, unless symptoms or the clinical context require more immediate evaluation.

Review medications, supplements, trauma, injections, seizures, thyroid status and other systemic causes. Ask about weakness, cramps, exertional intolerance, pigmenturia and family history.

Dark urine, severe pain, rapidly progressive weakness or metabolic instability is not an incidental-asymptomatic pathway and requires prompt assessment.

Use a Modern Stepwise Workup

**Persistent unexplained elevation deserves phenotype-directed investigation.** The EAN 2024 guideline, published in 2026, recommends investigating persistent oligo/asymptomatic CK above about 1.5 times an appropriate ULN.

The pathway includes exclusion of neurogenic and nonneuromuscular causes, electrodiagnostics, targeted metabolic evaluation and appropriate muscle imaging/genetic testing; it does not mandate biopsy first in every patient.

Molecular testing can precede biopsy in suspected inherited disease. Tissue remains useful when genetics is uninformative or inflammatory/metabolic pathology is suspected. Explain that a variant of uncertain significance is not a confirmed cause. Interpret the threshold with validated laboratory and demographic context rather than attaching a diagnosis to any value outside one generic range.

Obtain muscle MRI and a broad genetic panel immediately: MRI and genetics can be useful for persistent unexplained hyperCKemia, but a single postexercise result should first be confirmed after rest and common contributors reviewed.

Obtain needle EMG and proceed to biopsy if it is irritable: Electrodiagnostics and selected biopsy have later roles, but exercise can transiently raise CK and cause misleading findings; confirm persistence before this invasive sequence.

Stop follow-up because a normal examination excludes inherited muscle disease: Inherited disorders can initially present through hyperCKemia without weakness, so unexplained persistent elevation still warrants evaluation after transient causes are addressed.

questions.question: After a crush injury, an adult has dark urine, CK 24,000 U/L and rising potassium. There is no pulmonary edema or initial anuria. Which strategy best fits initial management?
options: Use loop-diuretic-driven urine output as the main target before correcting perfusion
Start bicarbonate-driven urinary alkalinization with fluids titrated mainly to urine pH
Start prophylactic continuous renal replacement therapy to clear myoglobin
Prompt individualized crystalloid resuscitation with ECG, electrolyte, urine-output and renal monitoring
questions.explanation:
Initial Rhabdomyolysis Management

Correct answer: Prompt individualized crystalloid resuscitation with ECG, electrolyte, urine-output and renal monitoring

Treat Immediate Physiology

**Rhabdomyolysis releases muscle contents** and can cause AKI, hyperkalemia, acidosis and calcium/phosphate abnormalities. ECG and urgent potassium management are priorities when hyperkalemia is significant.

Start crystalloid according to perfusion, losses and cardiac/renal reserve. The AAST 2022 consensus gives approximately ==400 mL/hour== as a possible adult starting rate, then titrates rather than prescribing one fixed rate for all patients.

Suggested urine-output targets are approximately ==1–3 mL/kg/hour==, up to about ==300 mL/hour==, where achievable safely. Persistent anuria is a reason to reassess, not to force escalating fluid into overload.

Monitor Complications and the Cause

**Follow urine output, renal function, electrolytes and clinical volume status.** Serial CK helps establish the trajectory, but treatment decisions should not depend on CK alone.

Routine bicarbonate, mannitol or loop diuretics solely to prevent AKI is not recommended by the cited consensus. Renal replacement treats standard complications rather than serving as automatic prophylaxis for a high enzyme result.

Assess compartment syndrome and the initiating trauma, drug, heat, seizure or metabolic cause. Early hypocalcemia often does not need replacement unless symptomatic or required for cardiac stabilization in hyperkalemia; later calcium changes also require follow-up. Recurrent or disproportionate exertional episodes warrant investigation for an underlying muscle disorder after stabilization.

Use loop-diuretic-driven urine output as the main target before correcting perfusion: Diuretics can treat selected volume-overload states, but forcing urine output does not replace restoring appropriate perfusion and can mislead assessment of resuscitation.

Start bicarbonate-driven urinary alkalinization with fluids titrated mainly to urine pH: Bicarbonate may be appropriate for a separate indication, but routine urine alkalinization has not shown sufficient prevention benefit to replace physiology-directed crystalloid and complication monitoring.

Start prophylactic continuous renal replacement therapy to clear myoglobin: Renal replacement is appropriate for established indications such as refractory hyperkalemia or overload, not routine prophylaxis based on myoglobin or CK burden alone.

AAST rhabdomyolysis clinical consensus document, 2022 — https://tsaco.bmj.com/content/7/1/e000836

questions.question: A patient has subacute proximal weakness, violaceous eyelid discoloration and papules over the extensor MCP/PIP joints. Muscle biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Inclusion body myositis
Antisynthetase syndrome
Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
Dermatomyositis
questions.explanation:
Recognizing Dermatomyositis

Correct answer: Dermatomyositis

Integrate Skin, Muscle and Histology

**Gottron papules and heliotrope change** are important DM clues. Photo-distributed erythema, periungual abnormalities and scalp disease can provide additional support.

Muscle involvement is variable: clinically amyopathic or hypomyopathic disease can have little weakness or CK elevation. A normal enzyme result does not exclude the systemic implications of the cutaneous phenotype.

Perifascicular atrophy and appropriate myxovirus-resistance protein A staining support muscle pathology in context, but individual findings have imperfect sensitivity and vary by antibody subgroup.

Antibodies Organize Risk Rather Than Replace Examination

**Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic cutaneous-muscle DM**, while TIF1-gamma and NXP2 inform cancer-risk assessment, MDA5 highlights lung risk and SAE can accompany prominent skin/bulbar disease.

Interpret assay strength and phenotype together. A positive panel does not independently establish every associated complication or justify treating an asymptomatic test result as proven organ disease.

Assess swallowing, lung and cardiac symptoms and perform risk-directed cancer evaluation. Treatment generally combines glucocorticoids with an appropriate steroid-sparing strategy, rehabilitation and skin care; organ severity determines urgency. Differentiate DM from inherited or toxic myopathy before prolonged immunosuppression, and follow objective strength and function rather than CK alone.

Antibody | High-yield associated pattern | Qualification

Mi-2 | Classic cutaneous-muscle phenotype | Phenotype association does not establish every complication

TIF1-gamma | Cancer-risk assessment | A risk marker, not a cancer diagnosis

NXP2 | Included in IMACS high-risk factors | Association evidence differs across cohorts

MDA5 | Amyopathic/hypomyopathic disease and RP-ILD risk | Low CK cannot establish lung safety

SAE | Prominent skin disease; possible bulbar involvement | Interpret assay and phenotype together

Inclusion body myositis: IBM commonly causes slowly progressive finger-flexor and quadriceps weakness with a different biopsy pattern; the subacute proximal-rash presentation is less consistent.

Antisynthetase syndrome: Antisynthetase disease can overlap with myositis and skin findings, especially mechanic’s hands, but the characteristic heliotrope/Gottron distribution and perifascicular pattern strongly support DM.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy: IMNM often causes severe proximal weakness and marked CK elevation with necrosis/regeneration, but usually lacks this characteristic DM rash and predominant perifascicular pattern.

questions.question: A 57-year-old with newly diagnosed dermatomyositis has anti-TIF1-gamma antibodies and no known cancer. Which approach best reflects IMACS 2023 guidance?
options: Use the moderate-risk assessment pathway
Use routine age/sex-based screening without additional myositis-directed assessment
Classify the patient as high risk and arrange guideline-directed enhanced assessment alongside routine age/sex-appropriate screening
Use serial tumor markers as the primary enhanced-screening approach
questions.explanation:
Risk-Stratified Cancer Screening in Myositis

Correct answer: Classify the patient as high risk and arrange guideline-directed enhanced assessment alongside routine age/sex-appropriate screening

Risk Is Relative to the Myositis Population

**Dermatomyositis, anti-TIF1-gamma and onset after age 40** are high-risk factors in the IMACS framework. Two or more high-risk factors place an adult in the high-risk group.

Other high-risk features include anti-NXP2, persistent high disease activity, moderate/severe dysphagia and cutaneous necrosis or ulceration. Antibody associations have differing evidence strength and must be interpreted accordingly.

These strata compare risk within adult IIM; a standard-risk category does not mean absence of cancer risk or permission to omit routine population screening.

Match the Evaluation to the Framework

**Basic and enhanced assessment supplement country-specific screening.** Enhanced evaluation can include cross-sectional neck, thoracic, abdominal and pelvic imaging and appropriate sex-specific tests, avoiding redundant procedures.

Investigate red flags such as weight loss, smoking-related concern, unexplained fever or night sweats regardless of a nominal category. If initial high-risk evaluation is unrevealing, specialist-directed additional testing and follow-up may be appropriate.

Discuss benefits, incidental findings, radiation and local cancer epidemiology. A positive myositis antibody does not diagnose cancer, and screening is not a reason to withhold necessary treatment of dangerous muscle or lung disease. Reassess the plan as clinical features evolve rather than applying a tumor-marker-only shortcut.

Screening Interval

**High-risk adult IIM warrants basic and enhanced screening at diagnosis, followed by basic screening annually for three years** under IMACS 2023, in addition to routine population programmes.

These recommendations apply within the guideline disease-onset context and do not mean automatic annual whole-body CT indefinitely. Reassess symptoms, baseline results and local cancer epidemiology.

Use the moderate-risk assessment pathway: Moderate-risk pathways apply to a different combination of features; DM, TIF1-gamma and onset after forty already place this patient in the high-risk category.

Use routine age/sex-based screening without additional myositis-directed assessment: Routine screening remains essential but does not cover the additional IMACS recommendations for this patient’s multiple high-risk factors.

Use serial tumor markers as the primary enhanced-screening approach: Selected markers can form part of a broader protocol, but a marker-only strategy cannot replace clinical evaluation and appropriate imaging in high-risk myositis.

    • Other high-risk features include anti-NXP2, persistent high disease activity, moderate/severe dysphagia and cutaneous necrosis or ulceration. Antibody associations have differing evidence strength and must be interpreted accordingly.
    • These strata compare risk within adult IIM; a standard-risk category does not mean absence of cancer risk or permission to omit routine population screening.

Match the Evaluation to the Framework

  • Basic and enhanced assessment supplement country-specific screening. Enhanced evaluation can include cross-sectional neck, thoracic, abdominal and pelvic imaging and appropriate sex-specific tests, avoiding redundant procedures.
    • Investigate red flags such as weight loss, smoking-related concern, unexplained fever or night sweats regardless of a nominal category. If initial high-risk evaluation is unrevealing, specialist-directed additional testing and follow-up may be appropriate.
    • Discuss benefits, incidental findings, radiation and local cancer epidemiology. A positive myositis antibody does not diagnose cancer, and screening is not a reason to withhold necessary treatment of dangerous muscle or lung disease. Reassess the plan as clinical features evolve rather than applying a tumor-marker-only shortcut.

Screening Interval

  • High-risk adult IIM warrants basic and enhanced screening at diagnosis, followed by basic screening annually for three years under IMACS 2023, in addition to routine population programmes.
    • These recommendations apply within the guideline disease-onset context and do not mean automatic annual whole-body CT indefinitely. Reassess symptoms, baseline results and local cancer epidemiology.

Other Options

  • A — Use the moderate-risk assessment pathway: Moderate-risk pathways apply to a different combination of features; DM, TIF1-gamma and onset after forty already place this patient in the high-risk category.
  • B — Use routine age/sex-based screening without additional myositis-directed assessment: Routine screening remains essential but does not cover the additional IMACS recommendations for this patient’s multiple high-risk factors.
  • D — Use serial tumor markers as the primary enhanced-screening approach: Selected markers can form part of a broader protocol, but a marker-only strategy cannot replace clinical evaluation and appropriate imaging in high-risk myositis.

  • IMACS international myositis-associated cancer screening guideline, 2023
  • British Society for Rheumatology inflammatory myopathy management guideline, 2022

questions.question: A patient has proximal weakness, inflammatory arthritis, fissured hyperkeratotic fingertips and anti-Jo-1 antibodies. CK improves after initial therapy, but exertional dyspnea persists. Which assessment is most important next?
options: Assess deconditioning with an exercise program before obtaining lung tests
Measure respiratory pressures and defer parenchymal imaging pending those results
Obtain chest radiography and repeat CK before deciding whether HRCT is needed
Evaluate interstitial lung disease with HRCT and pulmonary function testing including gas transfer
questions.explanation:
Antisynthetase Disease Beyond the Muscle

Correct answer: Evaluate interstitial lung disease with HRCT and pulmonary function testing including gas transfer

An Incomplete Triad Is Still Possible

**Antisynthetase antibodies target aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases**, with Jo-1 the best-known example. Myositis, arthritis and ILD can appear at different times and need not all be present initially.

Mechanic’s hands, Raynaud phenomenon and fever can provide clues. Non-Jo-1 phenotypes may be lung dominant, so lack of marked weakness does not exclude the syndrome.

Interpret the antibody in clinical context and avoid classifying every positive assay as disease. Characterize lung involvement directly rather than estimating it from the CK.

Assess Pulmonary Severity and Competing Causes

**HRCT and PFTs, including FVC and DLCO**, help define parenchymal involvement and functional impairment. Consider oxygenation, exercise limitation and the pace of deterioration.

Respiratory-muscle weakness, infection, aspiration, cardiac disease and pulmonary vascular disease can also contribute. A low FVC alone cannot distinguish restrictive ILD from weak respiratory muscles.

Coordinate rheumatology/neurology and pulmonary care. Immunosuppressive selection depends on lung and muscle severity, toxicity and response; steroid monotherapy can be inadequate for significant ILD. Monitor symptoms, imaging and physiology as appropriate, with urgent reassessment for rapid decline rather than waiting for a scheduled enzyme check.

Assess deconditioning with an exercise program before obtaining lung tests: Deconditioning can contribute after illness, but significant ILD must be assessed before assigning persistent dyspnea to fitness alone in this syndrome.

Measure respiratory pressures and defer parenchymal imaging pending those results: Respiratory-muscle assessment can help, but should not delay direct ILD evaluation in a symptomatic high-risk antisynthetase phenotype.

Obtain chest radiography and repeat CK before deciding whether HRCT is needed: Radiography and CK may be useful context, but can miss lung disease or dissociate from lung activity; persistent dyspnea warrants more sensitive pulmonary assessment.

questions.question: A patient with cutaneous dermatomyositis, minimal weakness and anti-MDA5 antibodies develops rapidly worsening hypoxemia and new diffuse interstitial abnormalities over days. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Begin low-dose mycophenolate monotherapy with gradual outpatient titration
Begin glucocorticoid monotherapy and add another agent only after prolonged nonresponse
Begin antifibrotic monotherapy with interval outpatient HRCT
Urgent multidisciplinary RP-ILD evaluation and upfront combination immune therapy while assessing infection and transplant needs
questions.explanation:
Anti-MDA5 and Rapidly Progressive ILD

Correct answer: Urgent multidisciplinary RP-ILD evaluation and upfront combination immune therapy while assessing infection and transplant needs

A Dangerous Muscle–Lung Disconnect

**Anti-MDA5-associated disease can have severe lung involvement with little muscle weakness or CK elevation.** Cutaneous ulceration and palmar lesions may provide additional clues, but are not required in every case.

Rapidly rising oxygen requirements and new HRCT abnormalities are urgent. Assess infection, aspiration, edema, drug toxicity and other competing processes in parallel rather than assuming that every opacity is autoimmune.

Ferritin and other laboratory trends can inform severity, but no isolated biomarker should replace oxygenation, imaging, clinical trajectory or organ assessment.

Combination Treatment With Evidence Qualifications

**ACR/CHEST guidance conditionally favors upfront triple combination therapy for confirmed or suspected MDA5 RP-ILD over monotherapy.** This is a low-certainty, specialist-directed strategy, not one universally proven drug trio.

Regimens commonly combine glucocorticoids with selected agents such as a calcineurin inhibitor and cyclophosphamide, or other guideline-listed options according to patient factors and expertise.

Monitor infection, cytopenias, kidney/liver toxicity and other treatment risks, with appropriate preventive measures. Arrange early lung-transplant referral when suitable rather than waiting until all treatment options have failed. Oxygen and ventilatory support address current physiology while therapy is selected; urgent lung care must not depend on the onset of overt myositis.

Begin low-dose mycophenolate monotherapy with gradual outpatient titration: Mycophenolate can be useful in IIM-ILD, but delayed-onset low-dose monotherapy does not meet the urgency and combination-treatment needs of this RP-ILD presentation.

Begin glucocorticoid monotherapy and add another agent only after prolonged nonresponse: Staged monotherapy can fit selected less aggressive disease, but RP-ILD with suspected MDA5 warrants urgent combination treatment under the conditional guideline recommendation.

Begin antifibrotic monotherapy with interval outpatient HRCT: Antifibrotics have selected fibrosing-ILD roles, but do not substitute for urgent immune and supportive management of this rapidly deteriorating inflammatory syndrome.

questions.question: A patient has progressive proximal weakness and CK 9,800 U/L that remains markedly elevated eight weeks after statin withdrawal. Anti-HMGCR antibodies are strongly positive in the appropriate phenotype. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Glucocorticoid myopathy
Self-limited statin-associated muscle symptoms
Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
Inclusion body myositis
questions.explanation:
Persistent Weakness After Statin Withdrawal

Correct answer: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy

An Immune Process Can Outlast the Exposure

**Anti-HMGCR IMNM** often causes substantial proximal weakness and CK elevation. Statin exposure is a recognized association but is not required, particularly in younger patients.

The principal serologic groups include anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP and seronegative IMNM. Anti-SRP disease can be particularly severe; subgroup identification helps clinical interpretation and specialist treatment planning.

Biopsy typically shows necrosis and regeneration with relatively sparse inflammation, but the pattern is not unique to one cause. In a convincing antibody-positive clinical setting, biopsy may not always be necessary; uncertainty or discordance can still justify tissue evaluation.

Treat Ongoing Disease Rather Than Withdrawal Alone

**Stop the implicated statin and arrange specialist immune treatment** when active IMNM is established. Withdrawal alone is often insufficient, and early combination treatment may be needed to prevent irreversible damage.

Glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing therapy are commonly used; IVIG is particularly useful in selected anti-HMGCR disease, while other approaches are individualized by subgroup, severity and response.

Monitor objective strength, swallowing, respiratory function when relevant, CK and medication toxicity. Interpret antibody results in context rather than using a low-probability screening signal as proof. Coordinate a future lipid-lowering strategy that avoids unplanned re-exposure and addresses cardiovascular risk alongside the muscle disorder.

Glucocorticoid myopathy: Steroid myopathy usually has normal or only modest CK and lacks this antibody association; a relevant steroid exposure would also be needed to support it.

Self-limited statin-associated muscle symptoms: Ordinary toxic symptoms generally improve after withdrawal; persistent substantial CK elevation and progressive objective weakness with concordant HMGCR antibodies suggest immune disease.

Inclusion body myositis: IBM more often evolves slowly with finger-flexor and knee-extensor involvement, while the severe subacute proximal phenotype and HMGCR serology favor IMNM.

questions.question: A 68-year-old has four years of slowly progressive asymmetric weakness, falls from knee buckling and difficulty gripping keys. Deep finger flexors and knee extensors are disproportionately weak; sensation is preserved. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy
Typical dermatomyositis
Sporadic inclusion body myositis
Multifocal motor neuropathy
questions.explanation:
Inclusion Body Myositis Pattern

Correct answer: Sporadic inclusion body myositis

Recognize Selective Weakness

**Deep finger-flexor and knee-extensor weakness**, often asymmetric, is a major IBM clue in an older adult. Dysphagia can be important and may not parallel limb disability.

CK is often normal to moderately elevated. EMG can contain mixed-looking units and irritability, so a neurogenic-appearing component should not automatically redirect the diagnosis to motor neuron disease.

Biopsy and the full clinicopathologic framework establish confidence. Endomysial inflammation, rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates and mitochondrial changes contribute, but not every feature is present in every sample.

Avoid Repeated Ineffective Immune Escalation

**Routine immunosuppression has not demonstrated the sustained benefit expected in many other immune myopathies.** Inflammation in tissue alone does not justify indefinite escalation without functional benefit.

Assess swallowing and aspiration, falls, mobility, hand function, nutrition and respiratory symptoms. Rehabilitation, assistive devices and appropriate exercise support quality of life and independence.

Anti-cN1A antibodies can support the diagnosis but have imperfect sensitivity and specificity and do not replace the phenotype and tissue assessment. The 2024 ENMC framework updates older criteria; do not demand an outdated relative-strength comparison as an absolute prerequisite. Discuss clinical trials where suitable while being clear about the limits of established disease-modifying treatment.

Anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy: HMGCR disease often causes marked CK elevation and more generalized proximal weakness; the distinctive chronic selective distribution is less characteristic.

Typical dermatomyositis: DM more often presents subacutely with symmetric proximal weakness and characteristic skin disease; the prolonged asymmetric finger-flexor/knee-extensor pattern favors IBM.

Multifocal motor neuropathy: MMN can cause asymmetric weakness without sensory loss, but follows named motor-nerve territories with supportive conduction findings rather than this characteristic selective muscle pattern.

questions.question: An adult has confirmed active non-IBM inflammatory myopathy with disabling proximal weakness but no immediate respiratory, swallowing or rapidly progressive lung emergency. Which general initial strategy is most appropriate?
options: Scheduled IVIG as the default first treatment for every inflammatory subtype
Azathioprine monotherapy with observation for its delayed effect
Glucocorticoid induction with an individualized steroid-sparing plan, rehabilitation and objective monitoring
Rehabilitation and symptomatic analgesia before initiating immune control
questions.explanation:
Initial Immune Treatment and Objective Follow-up

Correct answer: Glucocorticoid induction with an individualized steroid-sparing plan, rehabilitation and objective monitoring

Induce Control and Limit Cumulative Toxicity

**Glucocorticoids are standard induction treatment** for many active non-IBM inflammatory myopathies, with choice modified by subtype and organ severity. BSR 2022 describes adult oral prednisolone approximately ==0.5–1 mg/kg/day==, commonly ==40–60 mg/day==.

Severe disease may require intravenous therapy or additional rapid measures. A stable outpatient regimen should not be transferred to dangerous dysphagia, respiratory weakness or rapidly progressive ILD.

Agents such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate are selected according to phenotype, organ involvement, reproductive plans, contraindications and monitoring needs; no single agent suits every patient.

Measure More Than Muscle Enzymes

**Follow strength, function and extramuscular disease**, alongside CK and toxicity measures. Persistent weakness can reflect active inflammation, fixed damage, deconditioning, steroid myopathy or another diagnosis.

Provide supervised rehabilitation and appropriate exercise rather than prolonged indiscriminate inactivity. Assess nutrition, bone protection, infection risk, vaccination and drug-specific laboratory surveillance.

Escalate for a documented inadequate response after checking diagnosis, adherence, exposure and organ status. IVIG, rituximab or other therapies have selected roles, with evidence varying by subtype. An isolated enzyme change should not automatically trigger high-risk treatment or conceal worsening swallowing, lung disease or daily function.

Scheduled IVIG as the default first treatment for every inflammatory subtype: IVIG has important selected roles, including severe or refractory DM, but is not an interchangeable universal first-line regimen for all non-IBM inflammatory myopathies.

Azathioprine monotherapy with observation for its delayed effect: Azathioprine can provide steroid-sparing benefit, but delayed monotherapy is usually insufficient induction for disabling active muscle disease without a contraindication to glucocorticoids.

Rehabilitation and symptomatic analgesia before initiating immune control: Rehabilitation and pain care are important adjuncts, but do not replace treatment of confirmed disabling active immune muscle injury.

questions.question: Which statement accurately summarizes the ProDERM randomized trial in adults with active dermatomyositis?
options: IVIG was superior to rituximab for the week-16 composite response
IVIG 2 g/kg every four weeks improved the composite response rate at week 16 versus placebo
IVIG produced the same randomized benefit in inclusion body myositis
A single IVIG course established durable drug-free remission
questions.explanation:
What ProDERM Established

Correct answer: IVIG 2 g/kg every four weeks improved the composite response rate at week 16 versus placebo

Trial Population, Regimen and Endpoint

**ProDERM was a phase 3 placebo-controlled study of adult active DM.** During the 16-week randomized phase, patients received IVIG ==2 g/kg every four weeks== or placebo.

The primary response used at least minimal improvement on the Total Improvement Score, not an isolated laboratory threshold. Response occurred in approximately ==79%== versus ==44%== at week 16.

The study supports an IVIG role in this population, but does not establish universal response, cure, or superiority to every other immune strategy.

Benefit Must Be Balanced Against Infusion Risk

**Thromboembolic events were an important safety finding.** Assess thrombosis, renal, volume, hemolysis and infusion-related risks before treatment and monitor according to the product and patient.

Consider dose administration over appropriate days and infusion-rate precautions. New headache, chest pain, focal neurologic symptoms or renal deterioration requires assessment rather than automatic attribution to benign infusion discomfort.

Use objective clinical response to decide ongoing treatment and the broader steroid-sparing plan. A positive DM trial does not justify IVIG for an unsupported inflammatory diagnosis or every chronic weakness syndrome. The duration, background treatment and selected trial population define what can reasonably be inferred from the result.

IVIG was superior to rituximab for the week-16 composite response: ProDERM was placebo controlled, so it cannot establish superiority to an active rituximab regimen that was not its randomized comparator.

IVIG produced the same randomized benefit in inclusion body myositis: The population had adult DM; a different disease phenotype cannot inherit the same trial conclusion without its own evidence.

A single IVIG course established durable drug-free remission: The randomized phase used repeated four-weekly treatment and measured composite response at sixteen weeks; it did not demonstrate durable remission after one isolated course.

ProDERM randomized trial of IVIG in adult dermatomyositis, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2117912

British Society for Rheumatology inflammatory myopathy management guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/rheumatology/keac115

questions.question: A woman is found to carry her son’s pathogenic DMD variant. She has no weakness, dyspnea or cardiac symptoms. Which management is appropriate?
options: Arrange baseline cardiac assessment and ongoing surveillance despite absent skeletal symptoms
Reproductive counseling with cardiac evaluation only if symptoms emerge
Annual CK surveillance with cardiac imaging triggered by a rising CK
A one-time baseline ECG with no further testing if it is normal
questions.explanation:
Cardiac Risk in a Female DMD Variant Carrier

Correct answer: Arrange baseline cardiac assessment and ongoing surveillance despite absent skeletal symptoms

A Spectrum Rather Than a Male-Only Disorder

**Dystrophinopathies include Duchenne, Becker and predominantly cardiac presentations.** Severity and age at onset vary, and women with a pathogenic variant can also develop clinically important disease.

Duchenne usually presents earlier with more severe progressive weakness; Becker often retains more dystrophin function and has a later course, but cardiac disease can be disproportionate to limb disability.

Molecular testing should detect the relevant DMD variant type, including deletion/duplication when appropriate. A negative generic sequencing result is not equivalent to exclusion of all copy-number changes.

Surveillance Follows Organ Risk

**Evaluate the heart independently of reported muscle strength**, using cardiology assessment, ECG and appropriate imaging with periodic follow-up. Tailor intervals to age, findings and current specialty recommendations.

Affected patients also need respiratory, swallowing, rehabilitation, contracture, nutritional and bone assessment according to phenotype. Cardiac and respiratory decline may be clinically silent before advanced disease.

Offer counseling and cascade testing for the established familial variant. Discuss pregnancy with cardiac review where relevant. Genotype-specific and gene-directed treatments have changing eligibility and safety requirements; do not infer candidacy solely from the Duchenne label or substitute an emerging therapy for multidisciplinary surveillance.

Reproductive counseling with cardiac evaluation only if symptoms emerge: Counseling is necessary, but symptoms alone can miss early cardiomyopathy in a heterozygous woman; baseline and ongoing organ assessment are appropriate.

Annual CK surveillance with cardiac imaging triggered by a rising CK: CK can help describe skeletal involvement but cannot reliably gate cardiac risk; heart disease may occur without a parallel skeletal enzyme change.

A one-time baseline ECG with no further testing if it is normal: An initial ECG is useful, but does not exclude evolving structural disease or remove the need for a longitudinal cardiac assessment plan.

GeneReviews: dystrophinopathies, updated 2026 — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1119/

AAN/AANEM limb-girdle and distal dystrophy guideline, 2014 — https://www.aanem.org/docs/default-source/documents/lgmd_guideline-pdf.pdf

questions.question: A young adult has asymmetric scapular winging, weak eye closure, difficulty whistling and relatively preserved deltoid strength. Routine exome sequencing is unrevealing. Which next test most directly addresses the suspected disorder?
options: DMD deletion/duplication and sequence analysis
DMPK CTG-repeat expansion testing
Specialized D4Z4 repeat-array and permissive-haplotype assessment for FSHD
PABPN1 repeat analysis
questions.explanation:
FSHD Requires the Right Molecular Test

Correct answer: Specialized D4Z4 repeat-array and permissive-haplotype assessment for FSHD

Recognize the Selective Distribution

**FSHD commonly affects facial, scapular-stabilizing and upper-arm muscles**, often asymmetrically. Abdominal weakness and foot dorsiflexor involvement may add diagnostic clues.

Sensory loss is not a defining feature, and fixed weakness differs from the fluctuating fatigability of MG. Phenotypic variability and reduced penetrance can obscure family history.

CK may be normal or mildly elevated. Neither CK nor routine EMG provides the repeat-array and epigenetic information needed for a molecular diagnosis.

Repeat Structure and Haplotype Matter

**FSHD1 involves a pathogenic D4Z4 contraction on a permissive chromosome-4 background.** A routine exome may not resolve the repeat architecture, so an unrevealing result does not exclude FSHD.

If contraction testing is negative despite a convincing phenotype, specialized assessment can include methylation and FSHD2-related testing. Interpret repeat size, haplotype and epigenetic findings through an experienced laboratory.

Provide genetic counseling, rehabilitation and assessment for respiratory compromise when indicated. Selected patients also need hearing or retinal evaluation according to phenotype and guidance. Do not assume one inheritance pattern or one simple sequence variant explains every molecular subtype; testing limitations should be explicit before declaring the case genetically negative.

DMD deletion/duplication and sequence analysis: Dystrophin testing fits an X-linked dystrophinopathy phenotype, often with substantial CK elevation and a different distribution; it does not resolve the characteristic FSHD repeat mechanism.

DMPK CTG-repeat expansion testing: DMPK testing is appropriate for myotonic dystrophy with myotonia and systemic features; the asymmetric facial-scapular distribution instead directs testing toward FSHD.

PABPN1 repeat analysis: PABPN1 testing fits late-onset familial ptosis and dysphagia; the facial-scapular phenotype here is more characteristic of FSHD.

questions.question: An adult has progressive pelvic and shoulder-girdle weakness, elevated CK and no skin rash or sensory loss. Several relatives have unexplained muscle disease. Which diagnostic approach is best?
options: Start with one recessive-dystrophy gene selected from proximal weakness alone
Use phenotype, pedigree and associated organ findings to guide a suitably designed genetic evaluation
Start immune treatment and reserve molecular assessment for treatment failure
Perform biopsy first and assign inheritance from the histologic pattern
questions.explanation:
A Limb-Girdle Pattern Is Not One Genetic Diagnosis

Correct answer: Use phenotype, pedigree and associated organ findings to guide a suitably designed genetic evaluation

Describe the Phenotype Precisely

**Limb-girdle weakness is a pattern shared by many disorders.** Record age at onset, progression, scapular features, contractures, calf changes, distal involvement and exercise-related symptoms.

Pedigree and associated cardiac, respiratory or other systemic disease refine the differential. Consider dystrophinopathy, FSHD, Pompe disease and acquired myopathies when the pattern suggests them.

Modern nomenclature and gene associations evolve; a historical LGMD number should not replace molecular confirmation. Ensure testing includes relevant copy-number or other variant classes when needed.

Test and Protect Organs in Parallel

**Use appropriate panels or broader molecular assessment** when a single highly characteristic diagnosis is not established. Interpret uncertain variants through segregation, phenotype and other supporting data.

Muscle MRI, protein studies or biopsy can help when genetics is uninformative or an acquired/metabolic process remains possible. A negative panel only excludes what the assay can reliably detect.

Assess cardiac and respiratory risk before the gene is fully resolved when the phenotype warrants it. Symptoms can underestimate conduction disease or ventilatory impairment. Provide rehabilitation, safe exercise advice, contracture care and counseling while avoiding prolonged empirical immunosuppression based only on CK and proximal weakness.

Start with one recessive-dystrophy gene selected from proximal weakness alone: Single-gene testing can be efficient for a distinctive phenotype, but this broad distribution without subtype-specific clues does not identify one recessive cause.

Start immune treatment and reserve molecular assessment for treatment failure: Inflammatory disease requires supporting context; familial progressive weakness can be inherited, so empirical immune escalation should not delay an appropriate genetic evaluation.

Perform biopsy first and assign inheritance from the histologic pattern: Biopsy has selected diagnostic value, but similar dystrophic changes occur across genes and do not independently determine a pedigree or inheritance mechanism.

questions.question: A patient with grip myotonia, distal weakness and early cataracts has a pathogenic DMPK expansion. Before elective surgery, which issue most needs coordinated assessment beyond the limb examination?
options: Grip-relaxation timing and EMG discharge burden
Cardiac conduction disease and respiratory/anesthetic vulnerability
CK and conventional proximal-muscle EMG
Repeat-expansion size as the principal perioperative risk predictor
questions.explanation:
DM1: Myotonia Is Only One Part of the Risk

Correct answer: Cardiac conduction disease and respiratory/anesthetic vulnerability

A Multisystem Repeat-Expansion Disorder

**DM1 results from an expanded CTG repeat in DMPK** and is autosomal dominant. Myotonia, distal/facial weakness, cataracts and systemic manifestations can occur in varying combinations.

Repeat instability contributes to anticipation, but one blood repeat measurement does not precisely predict every organ outcome. Targeted expansion testing is needed; routine sequence analysis alone can miss the mechanism.

Congenital disease is a particular counseling concern, often through maternal transmission. Mildly affected relatives may remain unrecognized until a child or another family member is diagnosed.

Assess Silent Cardiorespiratory Disease

**Cardiac conduction defects and arrhythmias can occur without prominent symptoms.** Arrange ECG and appropriate cardiology surveillance, with further testing according to findings.

Evaluate respiratory muscle weakness, sleep-disordered breathing, swallowing and aspiration risk. Sedatives, opioids and anesthesia can expose limited reserve; use a disease-informed perioperative and postoperative plan.

Avoid assuming that an uneventful prior anesthetic guarantees safety. Monitor endocrine and metabolic features and provide rehabilitation and genetic counseling. Symptomatic antimyotonic treatment does not correct all multisystem risk and requires cardiac consideration; reducing stiffness is not equivalent to eliminating arrhythmia or respiratory vulnerability.

Grip-relaxation timing and EMG discharge burden: These characterize myotonia, but do not adequately assess silent conduction abnormalities, ventilatory reserve or sedative sensitivity before surgery.

CK and conventional proximal-muscle EMG: These may describe muscle disease but cannot substitute for cardiac and respiratory assessment in molecularly confirmed multisystem DM1.

Repeat-expansion size as the principal perioperative risk predictor: Repeat size informs the molecular diagnosis and broad counseling, but does not precisely predict individual cardiac, respiratory or anesthetic risk; direct organ assessment is needed.

questions.question: An adult has proximal weakness, prominent muscle pain, mild myotonia and early cataracts. DMPK expansion testing is negative. Which molecular test most directly evaluates the suspected alternative myotonic dystrophy?
options: CLCN1 sequence analysis alone
PABPN1 repeat analysis
D4Z4 repeat and haplotype analysis
CNBP CCTG-repeat expansion testing
questions.explanation:
DM2 and Repeat-Expansion Testing

Correct answer: CNBP CCTG-repeat expansion testing

A Proximal and Painful Myotonic Phenotype

**DM2 is associated with a CCTG expansion in CNBP** and usually follows autosomal dominant inheritance. Proximal or axial weakness and myalgia may be more conspicuous than clinical myotonia.

DM1 more often emphasizes distal/facial weakness and has a recognized congenital phenotype. These are useful tendencies, not absolute clinical rules for every individual.

Cataracts, metabolic abnormalities, cardiac involvement and other systemic features help distinguish dystrophic disease from isolated channel-related stiffness.

Use a Test That Can Detect the Mechanism

**A negative DMPK result does not exclude DM2.** Request a validated CNBP expansion assay; routine exome sequence analysis may not resolve the repeat adequately.

Interpret a molecular result with the phenotype and family history. Muscle biopsy can show overlapping features and is not a reliable substitute for distinguishing DM1 from DM2 genetically.

Assess cardiac conduction and function, respiratory/sleep symptoms, swallowing and endocrine status according to the patient. Manage pain, mobility and myotonia while accounting for drug and cardiac risks. Anesthesia requires a disease-informed plan even when myotonia is mild; a less severe limb phenotype does not establish absence of multisystem risk. Offer genetic counseling without applying DM1 repeat-size predictions indiscriminately to DM2.

Feature | DM1 | DM2

Gene/repeat | DMPK CTG | CNBP CCTG

Common weakness emphasis | Distal and facial | Proximal/axial; pain may be prominent

Myotonia | Often clinically evident | May be mild or less conspicuous

Shared concerns | Cardiac, respiratory, cataract, endocrine and anesthesia assessment | Cardiac, respiratory, cataract, endocrine and anesthesia assessment

Testing | Validated DMPK expansion assay | Validated CNBP expansion assay

CLCN1 sequence analysis alone: CLCN1 disease can cause nondystrophic myotonia, but progressive proximal weakness and early cataracts raise a multisystem myotonic dystrophy requiring expansion testing.

PABPN1 repeat analysis: PABPN1-related OPMD usually emphasizes later-onset ptosis and dysphagia rather than this myotonic, painful proximal phenotype with cataracts.

D4Z4 repeat and haplotype analysis: This addresses FSHD, typically suggested by selective facial-scapular weakness and asymmetry rather than myotonia and the multisystem dystrophic pattern here.

questions.question: A patient has years of slowly progressive bilateral ptosis and fixed external ophthalmoplegia, hearing impairment and exercise intolerance. MG evaluation is unrevealing. Blood testing for a mitochondrial DNA deletion is negative. Which interpretation is best?
options: Mitochondrial disease remains possible; specialized tissue-aware mtDNA and nuclear-gene evaluation may be needed
Repeat the identical blood deletion assay as the sole next investigation
Treat as seronegative MG on the basis of ptosis alone
Restrict further testing to maternally inherited point mutations in blood
questions.explanation:
Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia and Tissue Testing

Correct answer: Mitochondrial disease remains possible; specialized tissue-aware mtDNA and nuclear-gene evaluation may be needed

Look Beyond the Ocular Muscles

**CPEO is a phenotype rather than one molecular diagnosis.** Ptosis and relatively fixed progressive extraocular weakness can accompany exercise intolerance, hearing loss and other mitochondrial manifestations.

Ask about neuropathy, ataxia, pigmentary retinal change, endocrine features and cardiac symptoms. Conduction disease can be clinically important in deletion-associated multisystem syndromes.

Distinguish a slowly progressive myopathic ocular pattern from fluctuating MG, restrictive orbitopathy and focal cranial neuropathy. Normal CK or lactate does not exclude every mitochondrial presentation.

Match the Specimen to the Question

**mtDNA heteroplasmy varies among tissues.** Depending on age, phenotype and suspected variant, urine or muscle testing can add information not captured in blood.

Specialist molecular evaluation may need deletion analysis, sequencing and assessment of nuclear genes involved in mtDNA maintenance. A biopsy, when indicated, should be coordinated for the appropriate histochemical and molecular studies.

Assess cardiac, respiratory, swallowing, endocrine and hearing needs while testing proceeds. Genetic counseling follows the established molecular mechanism; maternal inheritance is not an adequate blanket explanation for nuclear mitochondrial disorders or every large deletion. Avoid declaring a molecular diagnosis from ragged-red fibers alone or excluding disease from one negative blood result.

Repeat the identical blood deletion assay as the sole next investigation: Repeat testing can address sample-quality concerns, but a sensitive negative blood assay may reflect tissue distribution or a nuclear cause; repeating it alone may leave the key limitation unresolved.

Treat as seronegative MG on the basis of ptosis alone: Ptosis occurs in both groups, but fixed progressive ophthalmoplegia with multisystem clues and unrevealing MG evaluation warrants targeted mitochondrial reassessment before immune treatment.

Restrict further testing to maternally inherited point mutations in blood: Mitochondrial ophthalmoplegia can involve large deletions, multiple deletions or nuclear genes, so limiting testing to one mutation category and specimen is inadequate.

questions.question: A 56-year-old has slowly progressive bilateral ptosis and dysphagia. His father and paternal aunt had similar late-onset symptoms. There is little day-to-day fluctuation and sensation is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: PABPN1-related oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
MuSK-positive myasthenia gravis
Myotonic dystrophy type 1
Sporadic inclusion body myositis
questions.explanation:
Oculopharyngeal Muscular Dystrophy and Aspiration

Correct answer: PABPN1-related oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy

A Late-Onset Inherited Oculopharyngeal Pattern

**OPMD is commonly associated with a pathogenic PABPN1 repeat expansion.** Ptosis and dysphagia often dominate early, with proximal limb weakness appearing in some patients.

Autosomal dominant transmission is common, although other inheritance contexts exist. Molecular confirmation should use an assay appropriate to the repeat mechanism and family findings.

The clinical pattern distinguishes it from an acquired fluctuating NMJ syndrome, but evaluate uncertain or atypical findings rather than assuming every familial swallowing problem has the same cause.

Swallowing Function Drives Important Morbidity

**Assess aspiration, nutritional intake and weight**, using speech/swallow expertise and instrumental evaluation when indicated. A patient may adapt eating habits and underreport severity.

Diet texture, compensatory strategies and nutritional support are individualized. Selected cricopharyngeal interventions can improve symptoms, but require specialist selection and do not eliminate the progressive muscle disorder.

Evaluate respiratory status and sleep-related symptoms according to phenotype, and plan ptosis procedures with attention to ocular protection. Genetic counseling and family assessment accompany rehabilitation. Do not delay aspiration management while awaiting a genetic result, and do not substitute repeated immune escalation for care of a confirmed inherited dystrophy.

MuSK-positive myasthenia gravis: MuSK MG can cause severe bulbar weakness, but the fixed late-onset familial ptosis-dysphagia pattern without clear fluctuation more strongly suggests OPMD.

Myotonic dystrophy type 1: DM1 can cause facial and bulbar weakness but often adds myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts and other systemic clues; this selective familial oculopharyngeal course favors OPMD.

Sporadic inclusion body myositis: IBM can cause dysphagia in this age range, but characteristic finger-flexor and knee-extensor weakness would be expected; the familial ptosis-led pattern suggests another disorder.

questions.question: An adult with molecularly confirmed POLG-related mitochondrial disease develops epilepsy. Which antiseizure drug should be avoided because of the specific risk of severe hepatic toxicity?
options: Valproate
Levetiracetam
Lamotrigine
Lacosamide
questions.explanation:
Valproate Risk in POLG Disease

Correct answer: Valproate

A Genotype-Specific Medication Hazard

**Valproate can precipitate severe or fatal hepatic dysfunction in POLG-related disease.** Its avoidance is a specific high-yield implication of identifying the molecular cause.

POLG is a nuclear gene involved in mitochondrial DNA maintenance. Its phenotypes can include epilepsy, ataxia, neuropathy and ophthalmoplegia; not every patient has the same syndrome or organ burden.

The precaution should not be diluted to routine enzyme monitoring as if standard-dose valproate were safe once tests are normal.

Treat Seizures Without Overgeneralizing Mitochondrial Risk

**Select an alternative by seizure type, organ function and interactions**, with specialist input. Acute status epilepticus still needs prompt treatment and escalation, avoiding valproate in confirmed POLG disease.

The 2024 InterERNs consensus distinguishes this contraindication from non-POLG mitochondrial disorders, where choices depend on the individual context. It does not prohibit every standard antiseizure medicine solely because a disorder is mitochondrial.

Counsel about inheritance using the established nuclear-gene mechanism rather than assuming maternal transmission. Review liver, cardiac, respiratory and nutritional issues and avoid catabolic stress where possible. Coordinate medication and procedure planning across specialties; symptom-directed care and genetic diagnosis should inform one another rather than leaving important safety information confined to a laboratory report.

Levetiracetam: Levetiracetam is a possible seizure-type-appropriate option in mitochondrial epilepsy and does not share the specific POLG-associated valproate contraindication; renal and behavioral factors still matter.

Lamotrigine: Lamotrigine may be used in suitable epilepsy contexts with careful titration and seizure-type review; it does not carry the same POLG-specific hepatic prohibition as valproate.

Lacosamide: Lacosamide can be considered for appropriate focal epilepsy with cardiac and other patient-specific precautions, but is not the drug with the characteristic POLG-related liver-failure risk.

GeneReviews: POLG-related disorders — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK26471/

InterERNs consensus on seizure management in primary mitochondrial disease, 2024 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11235721/

Review liver, cardiac, respiratory and nutritional issues and avoid catabolic stress where possible. questions.question: An adult has progressive limb-girdle and axial weakness with early diaphragmatic involvement and a marked fall in supine FVC. Sensation is normal and CK is moderately elevated. Which targeted investigation is most appropriate for a treatable metabolic cause?
options: Acid alpha-glucosidase activity screening followed by appropriate biochemical and GAA genetic confirmation
PYGM testing as the first phenotype-directed test
CPT2 testing as the first phenotype-directed test
Anti-HMGCR testing as the sole metabolic confirmation
questions.explanation:
Late-Onset Pompe Disease

Correct answer: Acid alpha-glucosidase activity screening followed by appropriate biochemical and GAA genetic confirmation

Respiratory Weakness Can Be Disproportionate

**Late-onset Pompe disease is a GAA-related lysosomal glycogen disorder.** Limb-girdle and axial weakness can coexist with diaphragmatic dysfunction before profound loss of ambulation.

Evaluate sitting and supine respiratory function, sleep-related hypoventilation, cough and swallowing. A patient’s preserved ability to walk does not establish adequate ventilatory reserve.

CK and EMG can be variably abnormal. A generic muscular dystrophy label should not prevent testing for this treatable alternative when the distribution and respiratory involvement fit.

Confirm Before Disease-Specific Treatment

**Dried-blood-spot GAA testing can be an initial screen**, followed by confirmation through appropriate enzymology and molecular assessment. Pseudodeficiency and sample quality can complicate a low screening result.

Biallelic pathogenic GAA variants and concordant deficient enzyme activity establish confidence; an isolated variant of uncertain significance or one low screening value should not be overinterpreted.

Refer for disease-specific enzyme-replacement assessment and multidisciplinary respiratory/rehabilitation care. Product selection, eligibility, infusion reactions and antibody issues require specialist review. Treatment can slow or improve aspects of disease but does not eliminate the need for ventilatory support when indicated; do not delay that support while awaiting molecular completion.

PYGM testing as the first phenotype-directed test: PYGM-related McArdle disease usually emphasizes early exercise cramps and second wind rather than this progressive axial-respiratory phenotype.

CPT2 testing as the first phenotype-directed test: Myopathic CPT II deficiency typically causes episodic exertional or fasting-related rhabdomyolysis with relative interepisode recovery, rather than this characteristic progressive respiratory weakness.

Anti-HMGCR testing as the sole metabolic confirmation: HMGCR antibodies investigate immune necrotizing myopathy, not a metabolic enzyme defect; they cannot confirm Pompe disease or replace appropriate enzyme/genetic evaluation.

questions.question: A young adult develops muscle cramps and marked fatigue during the first minutes of exercise. After slowing or briefly resting, activity becomes easier; occasional dark urine follows intense exertion. Which disorder best fits?
options: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency due to PYGM variants
Muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency due to PFKM variants
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency
questions.explanation:
McArdle Disease and Second Wind

Correct answer: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency due to PYGM variants

Blocked Muscle Glycogen Use

**McArdle disease is GSD V**, usually caused by biallelic PYGM variants. Failure to access muscle glycogen limits early exercise energy supply.

The second-wind phenomenon reflects improved tolerance as circulating fuels become more available. It is a useful clinical clue, but severe pain should not be pushed through to demonstrate it.

Rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria can occur, with AKI risk. Resting CK is often elevated; molecular confirmation is preferable to unnecessary hazardous provocation.

Plan Activity Rather Than Avoid All Exercise

**Gradual aerobic conditioning and recognition of early warning symptoms** can improve function. Avoid sudden intense or sustained isometric effort that provokes severe pain or contracture.

Selected pre-exercise carbohydrate intake can improve tolerance under an individualized dietary plan. Do not transfer this advice automatically to GSD VII, where a different metabolic block changes the response.

If a forearm exercise test is needed, use an appropriate nonischemic protocol in experienced hands; ischemic testing can provoke injury. Manage dark urine or severe pain as possible rhabdomyolysis rather than routine postexercise soreness. Provide education, genetic counseling and a safe activity plan that balances fitness, weight and injury prevention.

Disorder | Typical trigger or course | Diagnostic direction

McArdle / GSD V | Early exercise cramps; second wind | PYGM-related muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency

CPT II deficiency | Prolonged exercise, fasting or illness; episodic rhabdomyolysis | CPT2 testing / appropriate enzymology

Late-onset Pompe | Progressive axial/limb-girdle and respiratory weakness | GAA activity with biochemical/genetic confirmation

Tarui / GSD VII | Exercise intolerance; different response to carbohydrate | PFKM-related phosphofructokinase deficiency

Muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency due to PFKM variants: Tarui disease also causes exercise intolerance, but does not share the typical McArdle second-wind response and may include hemolysis; carbohydrate strategy also differs.

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency: CPT II disease is more associated with prolonged exercise, fasting, illness or cold-triggered rhabdomyolysis than the early exercise limitation with characteristic second wind.

Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency: Pompe disease commonly causes progressive limb-girdle/axial and respiratory weakness rather than the early-exercise cramp and second-wind pattern described.

questions.question: An adult has recurrent myalgia and pigmenturia after prolonged hiking, especially when fasting or unwell. Strength and CK are nearly normal between episodes, and there is no second-wind history. Which inherited defect is most likely?
options: Late-onset Pompe disease
McArdle disease
CPT II deficiency
Primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis
questions.explanation:
CPT II Deficiency and Prolonged Exercise

Correct answer: CPT II deficiency

Long-Chain Fuel Use During Stress

**The myopathic form of CPT II deficiency** impairs long-chain fatty-acid use and often manifests during prolonged exercise, fasting, illness or cold exposure.

Interepisode examination and CK can be normal, so one normal outpatient measurement does not exclude the diagnosis. Ask specifically about triggers, duration and pigmenturia.

Acylcarnitine profiles can support the evaluation, often with long-chain abnormalities, but results depend on clinical state. Molecular CPT2 testing or appropriate enzyme studies provides confirmation.

Prevent Catabolism and Treat Acute Injury

**Avoid prolonged fasting and unplanned exhausting exertion**, with specialist nutritional and sick-day guidance. Maintain adequate energy intake during illness and procedures.

Acute rhabdomyolysis needs prompt assessment of potassium, renal function, hydration and urine output. A genetic explanation does not reduce the urgency of dangerous electrolyte or kidney complications.

Specialist long-term dietary or metabolic therapies are selected to the disorder and patient; generic high-fat exercise advice is inappropriate. Offer counseling and family assessment, and review anesthetic/procedural planning. Recurrent episodes merit etiologic evaluation even when the initial event had a plausible environmental trigger, because trigger avoidance alone may leave an inherited susceptibility unrecognized.

Late-onset Pompe disease: Pompe usually presents with progressive limb-girdle/axial and respiratory weakness, not predominantly episodic rhabdomyolysis with near-normal intervals.

McArdle disease: McArdle disease more typically causes symptoms early in exercise with second wind and often persistently elevated CK; prolonged fasting-related episodes fit fatty-acid oxidation disease better.

Primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis: Periodic paralysis causes episodic weakness associated with potassium shifts, but recurrent exertional myoglobinuria and muscle breakdown indicate a metabolic muscle-injury process instead.

Continuum: metabolic myopathies — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10563931/

questions.question: A patient with confirmed familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis develops typical limb weakness after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Potassium is 2.6 mmol/L, swallowing is safe and there is no arrhythmia or respiratory weakness. Which initial strategy is appropriate?
options: Start acetazolamide as the sole acute rescue
Give intravenous KCl as the initial route despite safe swallowing and stable physiology
Give a large potassium dose calculated from a total-body depletion formula
Cautious oral potassium chloride with serial potassium and clinical/ECG assessment
questions.explanation:
Potassium During Familial Hypokalemic Paralysis

Correct answer: Cautious oral potassium chloride with serial potassium and clinical/ECG assessment

A Shift Is Different From a Depleted Store

**Familial hypoPP commonly involves CACNA1S or SCN4A channel dysfunction**, with attacks after carbohydrate loads or rest following exercise. Sensation and consciousness are generally preserved.

Measure potassium during weakness and assess ECG, breathing and swallowing. Exclude renal/GI losses, thyroid disease and other secondary causes when the presentation is not already securely characterized.

Low potassium contributes to membrane inexcitability, but total-body potassium is not usually depleted in a classic redistribution attack. This changes the safety of replacement.

Titrate Rather Than Replace an Assumed Deficit

**Oral KCl is preferred when the patient is stable and can swallow.** One expert-review approach uses ==0.2–0.4 mEq/kg== increments with reassessment; the exact protocol and repeat dosing require supervised monitoring.

Severe arrhythmia, unsafe swallowing or respiratory involvement may require monitored intravenous treatment and higher-level care. Avoid glucose-containing rescue fluids that intensify the potassium shift.

Watch for rebound hyperkalemia as strength returns. Long-term trigger modification and preventive medication are individualized by genotype, response and adverse effects; some sodium-channel variants respond poorly to acetazolamide. Do not use hazardous potassium/glucose provocation routinely to reproduce an attack when safer clinical, electrophysiologic and molecular evidence is available.

Start acetazolamide as the sole acute rescue: Acetazolamide has a genotype-dependent preventive role, but does not replace correction and monitoring of significant potassium abnormalities during an established attack.

Give intravenous KCl as the initial route despite safe swallowing and stable physiology: Intravenous therapy is appropriate for selected severe or unsafe-swallowing cases, but cautious oral dosing avoids unnecessary IV replacement risk in this stable attack.

Give a large potassium dose calculated from a total-body depletion formula: That framework can apply to genuine depletion, but a classic redistribution attack risks overshoot when the shift reverses; incremental reassessment is preferable.

Review of diagnosis and treatment of periodic paralysis, 2018 — https://periodicparalysis.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Statland-Dx-and-Rx-of-PP-Muscle-Nerve-2018-1.pdf

questions.question: A man develops acute flaccid weakness after a large meal. Potassium is 2.1 mmol/L, urinary potassium excretion is low, TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. Which management principle is most appropriate?
options: Use potassium replacement followed by long-term acetazolamide prophylaxis
Use monitored cautious potassium replacement, appropriate nonselective beta-blockade and definitive treatment of thyrotoxicosis
Use antithyroid therapy alone while observing the severe hypokalemia
Use large rapid potassium replacement as for a comparable depletion syndrome
questions.explanation:
Thyrotoxic Periodic Paralysis

Correct answer: Use monitored cautious potassium replacement, appropriate nonselective beta-blockade and definitive treatment of thyrotoxicosis

Look for Thyrotoxicosis Even When Signs Are Subtle

**TPP combines thyrotoxicosis with episodic weakness and intracellular potassium shift.** Overt tremor, weight loss or goiter may be less conspicuous than expected.

Low urinary potassium and the clinical context support redistribution rather than renal wasting. Evaluate magnesium, phosphate, ECG and competing causes of acute paralysis.

Carbohydrate loads and adrenergic stimuli can trigger attacks, but a family history is not required. Do not label every young patient with hypokalemic weakness as having a primary inherited channelopathy.

Reverse the Shift and Prevent Recurrence

**Nonselective beta-blockade can counter the adrenergic mechanism**, provided bradycardia, asthma, decompensated cardiac disease and other contraindications are considered.

Potassium is given cautiously with frequent checks and ECG monitoring according to severity. The cited review highlights greater rebound risk with larger replacement amounts, especially above about 50 mEq; this is not a universal safe/unsafe cutoff for every patient.

Treat the cause of thyrotoxicosis and maintain a prevention plan until euthyroid. Large potassium loads are not a substitute for that treatment. Acute respiratory compromise or arrhythmia requires urgent monitored care, and recovery of limb strength does not end electrolyte surveillance because overshoot can follow clinical improvement.

Use potassium replacement followed by long-term acetazolamide prophylaxis: This transfers a familial-paralysis preventive strategy without treating the thyroid driver; euthyroid control and cautious shift-directed acute management are central in TPP.

Use antithyroid therapy alone while observing the severe hypokalemia: Thyroid treatment prevents recurrence but takes time; marked hypokalemia and acute weakness also need immediate monitored management according to ECG and clinical severity.

Use large rapid potassium replacement as for a comparable depletion syndrome: Renal or GI depletion may require substantial replacement, but TPP mainly redistributes potassium and creates a rebound risk with aggressive dosing.

  • A — Use potassium replacement followed by long-term acetazolamide prophylaxis: This transfers a familial-paralysis preventive strategy without treating the thyroid driver; euthyroid control and cautious shift-directed acute management are central in TPP.
  • C — Use antithyroid therapy alone while observing the severe hypokalemia: Thyroid treatment prevents recurrence but takes time; marked hypokalemia and acute weakness also need immediate monitored management according to ECG and clinical severity.
  • D — Use large rapid potassium replacement as for a comparable depletion syndrome: Renal or GI depletion may require substantial replacement, but TPP mainly redistributes potassium and creates a rebound risk with aggressive dosing.
